• ISWG-GHG-23 IMO Papers from CSC and NGO

• MEPC 85 IMO Papers from CSC and NGO

Background:

The shipping sector makes up 2-3% of global greenhouse gas emissions – pumping 1 billion tonnes of GHGs into the atmosphere every year, comparable to the world’s fifth biggest emitting country, Japan. The IMO has committed to achieving its GHG Strategy goal, including its long-term goal of decarbonisation by 2050, its interim targets of a 30% reduction in absolute emissions by 2030 and 80% by 2040, and its commitment to a just and equitable transition.

The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.

title: IMO faces tough compromise on shipping emissions rules amid US opposition
summary: The IMO's Net-Zero Framework is again stalled, as US opposition to a global carbon pricing mechanism delays crucial financial penalties for high-emitting vessels. This ongoing political paralysis means polluters continue to operate with insufficient accountability for their carbon intensity. Without firm, mandatory fines for exceeding GHG limits, shipping's transition away from high-emission fuels remains dangerously slow.
content:
The International Maritime Organization faces another difficult round of negotiations over the Net-Zero Framework from late November, with countries seeking a compromise on the contentious carbon pricing mechanism that could determine the pace of shipping’s transition to low-carbon fuels.

While industry participants see growing agreement on the framework’s technical requirements for marine energy’s greenhouse gas emissions intensity, deep divisions remain over how ships should comply with the GHG standards, whether mandatory payments should be imposed for non-compliance, and how any revenues should be distributed.

The UN agency’s member states will meet Nov. 23-27 for technical negotiations, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session on Nov. 30-Dec. 3. An extraordinary session could resume Dec. 4 to consider adopting the framework.

The meetings follow a decision in October 2025 to postpone adoption for a year amid fierce US opposition to what Washington describes as a global carbon tax.

“I think it’s very hard to predict [the outcome],” Lloyd’s Register CEO Nick Brown told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. “Most of the concern is around the commercial instrument, because we don’t really have any experience of a global carbon tax that is applied across all countries, and how it is collected, and then what happens to the money.”

He suggested that governments could initially introduce technical requirements while gradually implementing financial measures.

“Maybe the economic measures could be introduced or phased in or ramped up over time,” Brown said.

Countries seek compromise

The framework approved in April 2025 combines progressively tightening GHG intensity thresholds from 2028 with financial penalties for ships failing to meet the requirements.

Under the original proposal, companies could comply by using lower-emission fuels, acquiring surplus units from other ships or purchasing remedial units, with payments directed into an IMO-managed fund.

The US has opposed mandatory payments, arguing that they would increase shipping costs and consumer inflation.

US Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella told Platts Nov. 11 that she expected countries to move toward consensus, although final rules might not be codified until 2027.

“I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027 it will be codified. But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus,” DiBella said.

Several countries have proposed alternative compliance arrangements.

China has suggested using multipliers to encourage uptake of zero or near-zero emission fuels, while Norway has proposed similar initiatives.

In separate proposals, Japan, Djibouti, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Somalia and Yemen have suggested ships could meet obligations through investments in maritime decarbonization projects rather than mandatory penalties.

Most EU and Pacific Island states continue to support the existing framework, although divisions have emerged within Europe.

Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Malta have called for pragmatic, cost-effective global measures, while Union of Greek Shipowners President Melina Travlos accused the EU of taking an uncompromising position that risked another negotiating deadlock.

“The EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end,” Travlos said in a Nov. 16 statement, questioning whether Brussels is more interested in preserving revenues generated from its Emissions Trading System for shipping and FuelEU maritime rather than pursuing a global framework.

The European Commission did not respond to emails seeking comment.

Compliance dilemma

Edmund Hughes, the International Bunker Industry Association’s representative to the IMO, said the central challenge was establishing a workable compliance mechanism for ships unable to obtain alternative fuels or sufficient surplus units.

“You can’t leave that void. It’s a void at the moment, and that’s where the impasse is … in the negotiation,” Hughes told Platts. “If you have a technical standard, you have to find a way to comply with it.”

Hughes said negotiators were attempting to balance environmental ambitions, commercial realities and political demands while preserving a framework acceptable to enough member states.

A coalition of nine shipping associations, including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping, IBIA and INTERTANKO, has urged governments to agree on enforceable global regulations that provide investment certainty and flexible compliance options.

The groups warned that fragmented regional rules could impose overlapping obligations and additional costs on shipping companies.

Separately, a group of shipowners, maritime associations and flag registries has called for an alternative global emissions framework that takes into account the availability and affordability of cleaner fuels, technological readiness and potential impacts on international trade.

The statement, circulated to media by Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry, was accompanied by a list of supporters that the ministry said represented approximately 55% of the international merchant fleet. The ministry stressed that the statement was industry-led and did not represent Saudi Arabia’s official position.

Environmental organizations, however, have cautioned against diluting the framework.

“The biggest danger at MEPC 85 is no longer delay, but a rushed deal designed to get Trump and his allies to the table,” said Alex Springer, deputy director of shipping at Transport & Environment.

Springer warned that concessions favoring fossil LNG and crop-based biofuels could prolong shipping’s dependence on fossil fuels.

Clean Shipping Coalition President Lucas Leppert urged countries to adopt the framework before year-end, arguing that further delays would undermine climate action.

Fuel demand implications

Whether and how IMO member states design the framework’s financial elements could affect the uptake of sustainable fuels, which remain more expensive than conventional, oil-based fuels due to limited availability.

October’s average delivered bunker costs in Singapore were $22.78/gigajoule for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil, compared with $27/GJ for B24 biofuel blends, $28.48/GJ for LNG and $48.47/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator.

“No shipping company is going to carry on buying more expensive fuel while their competitors are not,” Hughes said. “You need some way of closing that price gap.”

S&P Global Energy’s October 2026 Global Alternative Bunker Fuels Long-Term Outlook forecasts conventional fuel oil and gasoil’s share of bunker energy demand declining from 85% in 2030 to 26% by 2060, with shipping companies shifting to alternative fuels.

title: Time ticking: Two weeks for governments to green-light framework for cutting shipping emissions
summary: The IMO faces a two-week deadline to adopt its Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a mechanism previously deferred in October 2025. While proponents call it a "long-negotiated compromise," this framework remains a vague promise if it fails to mandate immediate, verifiable reductions in carbon intensity and HFO consumption. dirtiestships.com demands concrete regulatory teeth to penalize vessels exceeding their CII ratings, not just more bureaucratic delays.
content:
As a crucial fortnight of meetings opens at the International Maritime Organization opens in London, the Clean Shipping Coalition calls on member states of the UN’s shipping agency to back adoption without further delay of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) – the UN shipping body’s proposed mechanism for reducing shipping emissions.

Following the IMO’s deferral of a decision on the NZF in October 2025, the upcoming Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 23 Nov 23-27) and the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85, Nov 30-Dec 4), provide an opportunity to reaffirm commitment and a platform for adoption for this crucial framework.

The book is closed on further wrangling, it’s time for governments to show courage by taking action now to reduce shipping's climate heating emissions.”

“The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.”

“Since October 2025, when IMO member states voted to adjourn the adoption session for one year, various alternative proposals to the NZF were introduced and intensively discussed, but were neither able to demonstrate a comparable reduction in emissions nor gather sufficient support”, said Leppert. “These alternative proposals aimed at supplanting or distracting from the NZF have fallen away, proving the NZF as the best and only course ahead.”

“Pollution from shipping emissions is dirty and dangerous, causing an estimated 250,000 premature deaths and six million cases of child asthma each year and rivaling major industrialized economies in climate impacts”, said Delaine McCullough, Shipping Program Director at Ocean Conservancy. “Adopting the agreed upon Net-Zero Framework is the IMO’s quickest and most effective way to protect communities, address climate change, and create certainty for the shipping industry for decades to come.”

“The IMO has an opportunity to put shipping on a credible path to net zero, but ambition without accountability is just words on paper”, added McCullough. “The Net-Zero Framework must deliver meaningful emissions cuts, incentivize truly cleaner fuels, and generate funding to help countries make the transition. We need a deal that closes loopholes, prevents new fossil fuel lock-in and puts the resources behind the promises. title: Who Gets to Tax the Seas?
summary: The IMO's Net-Zero Framework proposes a global GHG emissions levy and dual clean-fuel standards, aiming for net-zero "by or around 2050" – a timeline as vague as its proposed market mechanism. Under this plan, ships failing increasingly stringent clean-fuel targets would pay escalating fees, yet researchers already doubt if these levies will adequately fund decarbonization or merely incentivize credit trading among polluters. As the IMO committee finalizes these rules, dirtiestships.com demands concrete, enforceable measures that genuinely penalize excessive carbon intensity, not just another bureaucratic exercise in greenwashing.
content:
What is the IMO, and why is there drama around it?

The International Maritime Organization (IMO), headquartered in a beige filing cabinet of a building on the south bank of the Thames in London, writes the rules for international shipping, from plastics to piracy, and each of its 176 members gets one vote. In 2023, members committed to cutting emissions in shipping to net zero “by or around 2050.” The plan to get there, known as the Net-Zero Framework, would amend the part of the IMO’s pollution treaty that covers air emissions to price the greenhouse gases ships emit by burning fossil fuels.

The framework covers the large ships (bigger than a Staten Island Ferry) that produce 85 percent of the industry’s emissions. It sets two clean-fuel standards, a lower bar and a higher bar, that rise every year and count emissions from a fuel’s production to its combustion. Ships that fall short of the higher bar would pay a fixed fee on the shortfall into an IMO-run fund, and ships that also miss the lower bar would pay more. Ships that outperform both bars would earn credits that they can sell to the worst performers to offset part of the heftier fee. In effect, ships that pollute more would subsidize those that pollute less. The fund would then reward the very cleanest ships and compensate poorer countries for the higher costs of shipping and the expense of transitioning to cleaner fuels. Some researchers, however, estimate that the fees may not even raise enough to pay out the clean-fuel rewards, much less fund the transition.

In April 2025, U.S. diplomats walked away from talks over the framework, threatening “reciprocal measures” against any country that backed it. Sixty-three delegations endorsed it anyway. By the next meeting, the Americans were back at the table with everyone else.

Next week, the IMO’s environment committee reconvenes to negotiate the precise set of rules that go up for a vote. If adopted, the IMO would become the first global regulator to make an entire industry pay for its emissions. That vote will test whether a multilateral agency can amass and allocate money that no member freely appropriated—and whether other countries can defy the United States, which would sooner sink this scheme than let others steer it.

Why does the United States object?

The United States objects more to taxes the U.S. Treasury Department neither collects nor spends than to taxing shipping at all. President Donald Trump has declared that “while I am president, there will be no global taxes,” meaning those imposed by an external revenue service. Under the Net-Zero Framework, shipping companies would pay into the fund directly, ultimately passing most of the costs on to cargo owners and consumers.

Americans would pay little, both relatively (because imports make up a small share of the U.S. economy) and absolutely (about $15 per American a year by 2030), but they would also get little back, because few U.S.-owned ships or clean-fuel producers would benefit from the incentives. The chair of the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission said in August that “any viable proposal” must count liquefied natural gas (LNG) toward compliance. That inclusion would drive demand for LNG from its top exporter, the United States—potentially tens of billions of dollars a year if, as she claims, that fuel supplies 60 percent of shipping by 2050.

The Trump administration’s objection to ceding authority to an international body is a familiar American refrain, particularly among Republicans. Officials entertain only voluntary arrangements, calling the framework a global tax “levied by an unaccountable UN organization” and a “global environmental slush fund.” At the same time, in October 2025, the administration began charging port fees on ships linked to China, and in February 2026, it announced a plan to charge every foreign-built ship calling at U.S. ports. These so-called trade remedies suggest that the administration rejects tax revenue set by others, not taxing shipping as such.

In fact, the United States has long refused to support funds whose choices it cannot veto, including in maritime regulation. In 1982, president Ronald Reagan refused to sign the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) because its seabed-mining regime would share revenue through a body in which the United States had no veto. The 1994 UNCLOS agreement that won president Bill Clinton’s signature secured that right. Trump’s objections differ more in degree than in kind from those of his predecessors, raising the question of why his administration has not yet quit the IMO, like so many other UN agencies.

Why hasn’t it quit?

The United States would gain little and lose much by leaving. At times, quitting has freed the country from its obligations—as with seabed mining, where the rules reach U.S. firms only with U.S. consent. But in this case, exit would spare the United States nothing, because enforcement runs through foreign ports: The treaty bars ports from treating nonparties’ ships more favorably, so once the world’s major trading hubs join the regime, compliance becomes a prerequisite for trade. Neither quitting nor withholding dues buys the United States a waiver. The Trump administration is bargaining for a carve-out instead of walking out, much like it did during negotiations over the global minimum tax, which would have let other countries tax U.S. firms regardless of U.S. participation.

Not quitting also keeps the Trump administration in a forum it values for other reasons. “Preserving freedom of navigation in all crucial sea lanes” is a top priority in the 2025 National Security Strategy. In his first statement to the IMO Council in July 2026, Ambassador Warren Stephens declared that the United States has “a profound stake in a rules-based maritime order” and pledged that “the United States has been—and will remain—a leading contributor to this organization.” He also cast the IMO as a venue to hold China accountable to the rule of law. But with just one vote, the United States must rely on others to get its way.

How can the Trump administration block a deal most members support?

Of the IMO’s 176 members, only the 108 bound by its air-emissions rules can vote to adopt the framework, and adoption needs two-thirds of those voting, so just over a third of the 108 can block. A motion to adjourn, which postpones the vote while keeping the text, takes a simple majority of votes cast by any of the 176 members. Adjourning draws votes from both sides, because framework supporters who fear losing the vote may prefer to wait, as when Singapore first suggested deferring the October 2025 vote, judging that delay “would best preserve the progress already made.”

Nor would adoption be the final word. Within ten months, one of two groups could band together to scuttle the framework by objecting: a third of the 108, or any coalition of the 108 that collectively hold half of world gross tonnage. Liberia, Panama, and the Marshall Islands alone—which agree that support for the framework “has continued to erode”—hold nearly half of the tonnage. Moreover, the United States is insisting on “explicit acceptance,” which means that the framework would bind only the governments that ratify it, and only once enough have done so. A minority, in other words, can be decisive.

In April 2025, only sixteen countries voted against the text, well short of a blocking third. In October 2025, fifty-seven voted to adjourn the meeting until December 4, 2026. In April 2026, fifty-one delegations argued for reopening the framework, which would restart the clock on adoption, against fifty-five. After that meeting, the State Department claimed “a total collapse in support for the original [Net-Zero Framework] proposal.” With so many demanding changes, the committee invited alternatives, opening a second path to delay: If a simple majority agrees to a substantive edit, the revised text must circulate for another six months. On November 11, the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission chair urged countries to keep submitting amendments.

Is the U.S. strategy working?

Yes, once American diplomats sat back down. Since then, the Trump administration has pressed from every level of government and recruited partners well beyond traditional U.S. allies, notably Saudi Arabia.

Much of Trump’s cabinet has declared that the United States would “not hesitate to retaliate” should others defy it at the IMO. Secretaries Marco Rubio, Chris Wright, and Sean Duffy also put IMO members “on notice” and promised penalties, from port bans on ships to limits on crew visas to sanctions on officials. In London last October, the pressure turned “very personal,” as U.S. representatives went “from delegation to delegation” threatening to limit visas for negotiators and their families, sometimes even during coffee breaks. They told Caribbean delegates they could be blacklisted, and they summoned European delegates to the U.S. embassy, threatening them with lost business. A veteran dealmaker compared the pressure to “dealing with the Mob.” Days before the October 2025 vote, the International Chamber of Shipping expected the framework to pass. Of the sixty-three countries that had approved it in April 2025, fifteen instead voted to adjourn, and ten abstained.

Since April 2026, open U.S. pressure has eased, because the administration no longer needs to defeat an adoption vote and can rely on vetoes other groups hold. Fossil fuel–producing countries supply the votes to adjourn or reopen the text, and flag-of-convenience countries can close ranks to object after any adoption. U.S. diplomats are also helping to draft a rewrite that reportedly drops the IMO fund and returns the fee money to dirty ships in the form of equity in clean-fuel projects. The clearest sign of whether the administration prefers compromise or indefinite delay will come not from the IMO’s December 4 vote but from whether its diplomats back a text that can come quickly to a vote at all.

What could happen before the vote?

The regularly scheduled IMO session ends on December 3, and it must first produce a text to vote on. If it does, the special session that adjourned in October 2025 will reconvene on December 4 to adopt the framework. If the regular session forwards the approved 2025 text with only updated dates, adoption could bring the framework into force as soon as spring 2028. Anything more ambitious than routine edits, however, involves more delay.

What does this mean for the future of U.S. multilateralism?

The United States has not uniformly abandoned international institutions so much as sorted them into those where quitting exempts Americans from undesirable rules, and those where quitting forfeits a spot in a desirable forum. The IMO showdown suggests that where the rules reach U.S. trade anyway, the Trump administration chooses to “get in there and fight, block, tackle, and win,” in the words of Ambassador Mike Waltz. December 4 will offer a sign of whether the administration can get more done by working through the IMO than around it, and of whether majority-rule bodies can impose a tax over a superpower’s objections.

Regardless, shipping will eventually pay for its pollution, if not through the IMO, then through another group’s carbon market. What is uncertain is whether the charges will be global or piecemeal, as levies that stall in international bodies are taken up by small clubs of willing nations. The European Union plans to credit shipowners for IMO payments if the framework is adopted and to review extending its own carbon market—into which shipowners already pay almost $10 billion annually—if it is not. In aviation, France, Spain, Kenya, and five other countries agreed in 2025 to each tax premium flyers nationally, outside the UN’s aviation agency. At COP31 this month, Guinea, Ivory Coast, and Mauritania each signed on to work toward charging ships for their emissions, like Djibouti and Gabon already do.

A similar patchwork outside the IMO would hurt poorer countries most and deepen lock-in to dirty fuels. Kenya’s climate envoy called the framework “necessary” to avoid such a patchwork of taxes “unilaterally imposed,” under which the poorest would still pay higher freight costs, resulting in losses of up to 0.4 percent of their GDP, while the revenue would flow into the treasuries of rich countries, with none returned. On November 18, nine trade groups spanning every sector of shipping implored the IMO to adopt one global rule, warning that such a patchwork would make ships pay twice and that “only global regulation can ensure a level playing field.”

Ultimately, obstruction may not spare U.S. trade the tax. Instead, it would move the revenue from a body in which the United States has one vote to clubs in which it has none. If the United States must pay either way, it does better helping decide where the money goes.

title: IMO study highlights major gaps in maritime climate finance
summary: The IMO's pilot study confirms a staggering USD 1.2 to 1.6 trillion capital investment gap for maritime decarbonization by 2050. Between 2018 and 2023, tracked maritime climate finance amounted to a mere USD 10.5 billion, representing only 0.14% of global climate finance. This glaring deficit implies an ongoing reliance on high-carbon fuels, ensuring current carbon intensity targets and FuelEU Maritime fines will remain a significant challenge for the industry.
content:
A pilot study published by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) under its GHG-SMART Programme, titled “Maritime Climate Finance Landscape: A pilot study of flows, gaps, and opportunities,” provides an initial assessment of where maritime climate finance is flowing, which activities are attracting investment and where significant gaps remain.

The report highlights three figures that illustrate the scale of the financing challenge:

USD 10.5 billion in direct maritime climate finance commitments were tracked between 2018 and 2023.

0.14% of tracked global climate finance was directed toward maritime activities during this period.

USD 1.2 trillion to USD 1.6 trillion in capital investment is estimated to be required for maritime decarbonization by 2050, covering vessels and supporting land-based infrastructure.

The broader investment requirements are not directly comparable with the narrower category of climate finance tracked by the pilot. Nevertheless, the findings highlight important differences in financing availability, investment priorities and regional participation.

The central issue is therefore not simply how much capital is available, but whether investments are appropriately coordinated, classified and structured to support the transition.

Key findings

1. Maritime climate finance is growing from a limited base

Tracked direct maritime climate finance reached USD 4.7 billion in 2023, more than doubling from the previous year. The report identifies a compound annual growth rate of 49% over the assessment period.

Nevertheless, the study cautions that growth has been uneven and influenced by a relatively small number of large projects. The available data do not yet establish a sustained long-term investment trend.

The relatively small maritime share of global climate finance indicates opportunities to attract additional capital, particularly as decarbonization technologies, infrastructure requirements and investment frameworks develop.

2. Investment is concentrated in alternative fuels and ports

The distribution of finance across the maritime value chain reveals significant differences between segments.

In 2023, alternative fuel production and distribution attracted USD 2.5 billion, while port infrastructure and operations received USD 1.4 billion. Together, these activities represented approximately 83% of direct maritime climate finance recorded that year.

By comparison, maritime operations and technologies, institutional strengthening, and particularly shipbuilding and recycling attracted substantially smaller recorded amounts.

This concentration partly reflects the considerable capital requirements of fuel production and land-based infrastructure. However, the report identifies a broader coordination challenge.

Investment in alternative fuel production requires confidence in future demand, while shipowners considering new propulsion technologies depend on fuel availability and suitable port infrastructure. Similarly, ports must assess expected vessel requirements before committing capital to new facilities.

The issue is also reflected in a recent Lloyd’s Register assessment highlighting the growing mismatch between fleet investment and fuel availability, which identifies uneven infrastructure development and the importance of linking investment to credible demand.

Without alignment between these decisions, the transition could face infrastructure mismatches, inefficient capital allocation and stranded-asset risks.

The study also finds that much upstream alternative fuel investment cannot currently be linked to identifiable maritime demand. Of USD 16.7 billion in combined direct and indirect finance tracked for alternative fuel production and distribution, approximately 85% could not be directly attributed to maritime use.

The findings highlight that increasing investment alone is insufficient without coordination between fuel supply, vessel development and port infrastructure.

3. Financing instruments differ significantly across markets

Public and private sources contributed broadly comparable shares of tracked maritime climate finance, but the financing instruments used varied considerably.

Market-rate debt accounted for 61% of recorded investment between 2018 and 2023. This financing was primarily associated with activities offering more established revenue models, larger asset bases or stronger access to commercial lending.

Equity played a more targeted role in emerging technologies and alternative fuel projects, while grants and concessional debt supported infrastructure development and activities with less mature commercial prospects.

These differences become particularly important when examining access to finance in developing countries.

Small island developing States (SIDS) and least developed countries (LDCs) relied predominantly on international public financing, principally through grants and low-cost debt. In contrast, advanced economies and other more commercially developed markets were better positioned to attract market-rate debt and private equity.

The report consequently emphasizes the need to match financing instruments with project maturity, investment risks, commercial viability and local economic circumstances.

The relevance of alternative financing structures is illustrated by a recent blended-finance initiative supporting wind-assisted propulsion on two vessels, designed to reduce upfront investment costs for energy-saving technologies.

This suggests that increasing the availability of capital may not be sufficient unless suitable financial mechanisms are also accessible to different markets.

4. Developing countries face unequal access to transition finance

The report identifies a significant distinction between financing for climate resilience and financing for emissions reduction in vulnerable countries.

SIDS and LDCs together received approximately 68% of tracked maritime adaptation finance between 2018 and 2023, predominantly supporting port infrastructure.

However, their participation in mitigation finance was substantially smaller, accounting for approximately 1.5% of the tracked global maritime mitigation total.

Investment reaching these countries for alternative fuel production and distribution was almost nonexistent in the tracked data, while financing for maritime operations and technologies remained limited.

This creates a distinction between investments that help maritime infrastructure withstand climate impacts and those that enable countries to participate in shipping’s decarbonization.

Similar challenges were identified in an earlier International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH) study examining climate resilience and decarbonization in developing-country ports, which highlighted the investment needs and financing constraints facing these facilities.

To address this imbalance, the IMO study recommends combining resilience and emissions-reduction objectives where appropriate, including through low-emission port infrastructure, vessel efficiency measures and suitable regional initiatives.

It also identifies opportunities to use blended finance, guarantees and risk-sharing arrangements to improve access to capital for projects that may otherwise struggle to attract commercial investment.

The findings underline the importance of financing approaches that address both the immediate resilience requirements of vulnerable countries and their longer-term participation in the maritime energy transition.

5. Inconsistent classification and reporting create additional challenges

A further finding concerns the difficulty of identifying and measuring maritime climate finance consistently.

The study reviewed 19 national and regional taxonomies and global frameworks, finding that maritime activities were covered unevenly.

Ship retrofits and low-emission vessels were relatively well represented, while shipbuilding, adaptation measures and enabling activities received less systematic recognition.

The problem is compounded by incomplete financial reporting. Domestic public expenditure, private investment in vessel retrofits and energy efficiency, and financing for shipbuilding and recycling are not consistently captured.

Consequently, low recorded finance in certain activities should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that equivalent investment is absent.

The report recommends clearer definitions, interoperable classification systems and more consistent project-level monitoring to improve the identification and assessment of maritime climate finance.

A recent development in this area is the adoption of the revised Singapore-Asia Taxonomy by FEET to support vessel retrofit financing, highlighting the role of standardized assessment and measurement in financing maritime decarbonization.

Such measures could help maritime organizations and financial institutions identify eligible investments, improve transparency and monitor financing outcomes more effectively.

title: World Shipping Council calls for global agreement on shipping emissions as industry investment surpasses $200 billion USD
summary: The World Shipping Council (WSC) demands global GHG regulations, warning that regulatory uncertainty hinders investment in "cleaner" fuels. While $200 billion is reportedly committed to 1,350 dual-fuel ships, many will continue burning fossil fuels like LNG, offering limited immediate carbon intensity reduction. dirtiestships.com remains skeptical; calls for regulation must include immediate, enforceable targets, not just pledges, to genuinely curb excessive HFO use and meet strict CII ratings.
content:
The World Shipping Council (WSC) is calling on governments to agree on binding global greenhouse gas regulations for international shipping without further delay, warning that continued uncertainty risks slowing investment in cleaner fuels and infrastructure.

As the next round of negotiations get underway at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), WSC has identified three elements it considers essential to an effective agreement that delivers on the commitments governments made under the 2023 GHG Strategy:

• A credible pathway to net zero, with clear and predictable emissions reduction requirements aligned with the IMO’s 2023 GHG Strategy’s ambition.

• Strong and consistent enforcement, ensuring the same rules apply to every ship from the first year.

• Incentives for cleaner fuels, helping close the price gap between conventional fuels and zero and near-zero greenhouse gas fuels.

The call builds on a joint statement issued by nine major international shipping associations, including WSC, ahead of the IMO negotiations. Representing the global commercial shipping fleet, the associations urged governments to agree on effective and enforceable global regulations that provide investment certainty, incentivise cleaner fuels and maintain a level playing field across international shipping.

For the liner industry specifically, investment is already well underway. Container shipping and vehicle carriers have committed more than USD $200 billion to over 1,350 dual-fuel ships, including over 500 already operating. These investments show the industry’s readiness to transition, but unlocking their full emissions reduction potential depends on the availability and commercial competitiveness of cleaner fuels.

“Shipping companies are investing billions in ships capable of running on cleaner fuels. We need global rules that give fuel producers and shipowners the confidence to invest in the next stage of the transition,” said Joe Kramek, President & CEO of WSC.

“Clear targets, effective enforcement and meaningful incentives for cleaner fuels must work together. An agreement that delivers all three can accelerate progress towards net zero and help turn the investment already underway into real emissions reductions.”

WSC cautions that further delays or a framework focused primarily on experience building or fuel market readiness would prolong uncertainty rather than support the transition.

Without a meaningful global framework, shipping risks facing a growing patchwork of national and regional emissions regulations, adding complexity and costs to international trade. Since the IMO’s decision to delay adoption of the global agreement, several national shipping carbon charging schemes have been introduced or advanced, underscoring the urgency of reaching a common global regulation.

“We believe IMO Member States can work together to reach an agreement that delivers on the commitments made in 2023. As an industry, we will be responsible for implementing the rules agreed at the IMO. That’s why we are calling for clear reduction targets, consistent enforcement and meaningful incentives for cleaner fuels. These are the foundations of an effective global framework that can deliver real emissions reductions,” said Joe Kramek.

title: Op-Ed: Why the UN's Shipping Agency Must Adopt Its Climate Agreement
summary: The IMO's Net-Zero Framework (NZF) adoption remains stalled by political maneuvers, exposing the shipping industry's chronic resistance to meaningful decarbonization. While proposing a 30% emissions reduction by 2030, this framework is merely a proposal, offering no immediate accountability for current carbon intensity or excessive HFO usage. As global climate impacts escalate, this persistent inaction proves the industry's "green goals" remain detached from urgent, enforceable reality.
content:
That pressure resulted in postponement. As this next IMO meeting approaches, momentous midterm elections have changed the country’s political landscape. For now, it remains unclear whether the US will return to the IMO with the same tactics.

title: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement
summary: China's 2024 "retire-and-renew" policy offers subsidies for older vessel replacement, ostensibly to accelerate fleet decarbonization. Crucially, the policy fails to mandate *which* fuels "new/clean energy vessels" must use, opening the door for continued fossil fuel reliance under a 'green' label. Without strict fuel mandates, this scheme risks becoming a fleet modernization program rather than a genuine driver for significant greenhouse gas reductions, failing to address core carbon intensity challenges.
content:
Maritime shipping plays a key role in China’s national freight sector, accounting for over 50% of transportation activity in 2024. Decarbonization of this sector at a rate in line with the government’s goal to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 will require the large-scale application of ships fueled by low- and zero-carbon fuels.

China introduced policies in 2024 to promote the scrapping and renewal of old ships, which offer shipowners tiered subsidies to renew older ships before their mandatory retirement dates, with greater support for new/clean energy vessels (NCEVs). However, the policy does not specify which fuels NCEVs must use.

This paper estimates the potential impact of the retire-and-renew (RNR) policy on fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions in China’s coastal fleet. Using the Vessel Economic Guidance and Assessment (VEGA) model and Polaris, a shipping emissions projection model, we estimated fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions from 2025 to 2050 under the existing RNR policy design and two alternative scenarios.

title: HMM Signs 'Green Sailing' Deal with NextPower; Emissions
summary: HMM is expanding its "Green Sailing" service, selling reported GHG emission reductions from "low-carbon fuel" usage to clients like NextPower for Scope 3 accounting. This financial mechanism allows clients to offset their indirect emissions, while HMM recovers costs for fuels often only marginally less carbon-intensive. Despite claims of "additionality," this scheme does not directly improve HMM's fleet-wide CII ratings or necessarily reduce its exposure to FuelEU Maritime fines beyond basic compliance.
content:
South Korea's HMM (011200) has signed a greenhouse gas emissions-reduction trading contract with U.S. renewable energy company NextPower, expanding the customer base for its "Green Sailing service" from logistics, distribution and fashion to the energy sector. HMM disclosed the signing on the 23rd.

The Green Sailing service is an eco-friendly offering in which a vessel transfers to a shipper the greenhouse gas reductions achieved by using low-carbon fuel during maritime transport. Shippers that receive the reductions can reflect them in the accounting and reporting of Scope 3 (indirect) emissions generated across their supply chains. HMM recovers part of the cost of adopting low-carbon fuel and reinvests it in eco-friendly fuel, establishing a virtuous cycle.

NextPower is a Nasdaq-listed company that supplies large-scale solar power facilities and smart energy solutions. Under the deal, NextPower can use the reductions transferred from HMM in managing its own indirect emissions. This marks the first time HMM's emissions-reduction counterparty has expanded from logistics, distribution and fashion companies to an energy company.

HMM applies two principles to ensure the credibility of its reductions. First, in line with the additionality principle set out by the Global Maritime Forum (GMF), it excludes reductions used to comply with legal obligations such as European Union (EU) environmental regulations and provides customers only with performance that voluntarily cuts emissions beyond those obligations. In addition, it secures objectivity through third-party verification and blocks double counting, in which the same performance is reflected redundantly across multiple customers. From the customer's perspective, verified reductions can be used in environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosures to enhance credibility and transparency.

HMM has steadily expanded its customers—starting with German logistics company Hellmann in 2023, followed by IKEA in 2024 and Nike last year—and has now added NextPower. "We plan to continue preemptive investments to cut greenhouse gases, including diversifying our adoption of low-carbon fuels," an HMM official said. "We will develop our eco-friendly policy into a new growth engine for the company."

The deal illustrates a trend in which the shipping industry's response to decarbonization regulations is moving beyond a cost burden to become a new revenue source. As greenhouse gas regulations from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the EU tighten, shippers are seeking ways to reduce supply chain emissions, and carriers are responding by offsetting the cost of low-carbon fuel investments through the sale of reductions. HMM's expansion of its counterparties to energy companies suggests that emissions reductions are becoming a general-purpose commodity not confined to a specific industry.

However, the emissions-reduction trading market is still in the process of standardization, so how consistently additionality is demonstrated and anti-double-counting systems are maintained is expected to determine the service's credibility. HMM plans to expand its supply of reductions by diversifying its low-carbon fuel sources while upgrading its verification system to gain an edge in the competition to secure global shippers.

title: Will e-methanol become a game changer for decarbonising maritime shipping and plastic industries?
summary: The Kassø plant will produce 42,000 tonnes of e-methanol annually, optimistically touted as a 'game changer' for maritime decarbonisation. This volume is negligible against global shipping's 200 million tonnes of annual fuel consumption and its persistent reliance on heavy fuel oil. Until dirty ships face severe FuelEU Maritime fines for their excessive emissions and consistently failing CII ratings, such projects remain a mere distraction from the urgent need for radical operational changes and immediate HFO reduction.
content:
When it comes to decarbonisation, some industries, such as maritime shipping and plastic production, are faced with serious problems. e-methanol could solve some of them.

Biogas from slurry, sustainable electricity from solar panels, water from a well; these are the ingredients needed to synthesise e-methanol. These are all processed within an impressive industrial jungle, made from intermingled steel tubes, imposing distillation towers and curiously flat storage tanks.

The first of its kind

While adjusting my hard hat, a huge truck enters the site. “Every day we receive 5 trailers with biogenic CO2”, Lars Dyrholm explains. Lars is not just one of those hardy Danish “Ironmen”, capable of running for many kilometres without losing breath. He is also the CEO of the Kassø site, supervising the upscaling of production in this first of its kind industrial plant.

Mia Amalie Jochimsem, an on-site employee, joins us. “We have so much agriculture around here”, she says, adding: “We capture the CO₂ from the biogas plants.” Dyrholm and Jochimsem take me on a tour of discovery through the innovative jungle of steel and pipes.

A European flagship project

But let’s start from the very beginning: “In here we have the electrolysers”, Jochimsem explains. “This is where water is separated into hydrogen and oxygen.” Once biogenic CO₂ is added, e-methanol is created.

The plant is a European flagship project. European Energy — a world-leading company in sustainable energy generation — is proving that methanol can be produced on a large-scale industrial basis without using fossil fuels. This, in turn, can be used for making plastics or fueling vessels.

“We are replacing the fossil-based fuels with something that’s green and renewable”, Lars Dyrholm says.

There’s more in the pipeline

The Kassø plant is built to produce 42,000 tonnes of e-methanol per year. “Right now, we are producing around 100 tonnes per day”, the Kassø CEO says. “So, we have two trucks of e-methanol leaving the site every day now.”

European Energy has ambitious plans. If the Member States of the European Union agree on a stable regulatory framework, further e-methanol plants could be built. A first step is the implementation of the EU’s Renewable Energy Directive.

The journey towards full decarbonisation

“A portion of the fuel used in road transportation first will be replaced with something that is renewable”, Lars Dyrholm explains. “This is driving up demand and also prices, enabling us to make further investments in plants like this in the future. And this is the journey right now towards decarbonisation by 2050, to be 100% fossil-free.

“But we also need regulatory certainty, long-term, that Europe sticks to these commitments and ambitions so that we can continue to produce renewable energy fuels in this journey towards full decarbonisation.” The EUFuel Maritime Regulation helps in this regard.

Negotiations at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), on the other hand, have been at a standstill since October 2025, after the Trump administration threatened to impose punitive tariffs on countries should they back the proposed Net-Zero Framework.

Huge ships and tiny hands

One of the biggest buyers of ‘green methanol’ is the Danish logistics group A.P. Moller-Maersk, which is converting parts of its fleet to sustainable fuels. But e-methanol can do more than just power ships across the world’s oceans.

I drive over to Billund, the Danish HQ of LEGO, the global toy giant. e-methanol is a raw material used to produce ePOM, a climate-friendly plastic, and is already being used to manufacture LEGO figurine’s tiny hands, small wheels, and connector elements.

There is still a long way to go

At industry conferences, European Energy presents a LEGO model of its e-methanol plant. I meet Knud Erik Andersen in the Danish capital, Copenhagen. He co-founded the company in 2004.

“Europe is a very strong continent”, he says. “But we still import around 60% of our energy. So, there is still a long way to go for replacing imports with home-grown energy from primarily renewable sources, so that we can be resilient and totally independent from foreign nations.”

Andersen has some strong ideas about how to create a flourishing market for green hydrogen and e-methanol: “The public sector in Europe could start to act as a customer by buying e-fuel for naval ships, for the defense industry.”

Half a million solar panels

Electrolysis requires enormous amounts of electricity. That is why European Energy has built its e-methanol plant right next to a massive solar park. “This is one of the biggest solar parks in Northern Europe, with a capacity of 300 MW”, European Energy manager Kristian Tilsted says.

Half a million solar panels generate the ‘green electrons’ needed to produce e-methanol. Not all of them are used in the facility, the rest are fed into a high-voltage grid.

Kristian Tilsted: “Our national grid is a kind of energy highway connected to the rest of Europe. Those green electrons can be used all over Europe in households or for industries. We are aiming at 100% green transition both here in Denmark, but also all over the world. And to be able to deliver on that, we need to build out the infrastructure — both locally but also in Europe.”

title: UK and EU Agree to Link Emissions Trading Schemes — Ship & Bunker
summary: The UK and EU Emissions Trading Schemes will link from January 1, 2028, with the UK scheme belatedly expanding to cover 50% of international voyage emissions, merely aligning with the EU's established scope. This integration, alongside the UK scrapping its auction reserve price, risks weakening the financial incentive for prompt decarbonization, given UK allowances' historical discount to EUAs. Specific derogations for island ro-pax and ice-class vessels until 2030 further highlight persistent loopholes, allowing certain fleets to delay meaningful emissions reductions.
content:
Link intended to be operational from January 1, 2028, with UK and EU allowances valid in either scheme

UK ETS to cover 50% of international voyage emissions from the same date

UK auction reserve price scrapped when the link goes live

Northern Ireland derogation goes, island ro-pax and ice-class derogations kept to end-2030

The UK and EU have agreed to link their emissions trading systems, with the link intended to be operational from January 1, 2028, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said in an explainer published on Friday.

From that date allowances issued under either scheme can be used for compliance in the other, including for 2027 emissions, with the first joint surrender deadline on September 30, 2028.

Operators should also be able to use one pool of allowances for both their UK and EU obligations, without needing to buy UK allowances (UKAs) and EU allowances (EUAs) separately, greatly simplifying compliance requirements for those on international voyages.

For shipping, the agreement confirms that the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) will expand to cover 50% of emissions from international voyages by ships of 5,000 GT and above from the same date, alongside the 100% of domestic and in-port emissions it has covered since July 1, 2026.

The expansion was first set out last November with the same January 1, 2028 start, so the UK's coverage of international shipping and the allowance link now begin together.

The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) already covers 50% of emissions on voyages between an EU port and a port outside the bloc.

As part of the move, the UK will remove its auction reserve price when the link goes live, since "it would not be practical or desirable to maintain a price floor in only one part of a linked market," the explainer says.

UK allowances have traded below EUAs since the scheme began, and earlier this year Ship & Bunker calculated an average discount of 21.8% in the first half of 2026.

Derogations

The agreement removes the temporary 50% surrender derogation for voyages between Northern Ireland and Great Britain, "as planned", so that all covered Irish Sea voyages face the same 100% obligation.

The UK will align with the EU's temporary derogation for passenger and ro-pax voyages to islands with fewer than 200,000 people and no road or rail link to the mainland, until at least December 31, 2030, and ice-class ships will get a 5% surrender derogation to the same date.

Shipping companies will be able to apply a zero emission factor to biofuels, RFNBOs and recycled carbon fuels that meet the Renewable Energy Directive's criteria.

Should a global measure be adopted at the IMO, the UK "will review its interactions with our own policy, to avoid any double charging of emissions", the document says.

That said, the IBIA Annual Convention in New York heard last week that the EU is unlikely to give up the ETS whatever the outcome on the IMO Net-Zero Framework, with Peter Keller, Chairman of SEA-LNG, saying: "What government do we know anywhere in the world is prepared to give up tax revenue?"

The deal came a day after the UK Chamber of Shipping called on both sides to use the reset talks to cut costs, asking for ETS revenues to support shipping's decarbonisation and for a full economic impact assessment before the UK ETS was extended internationally.

"We also need to see the revenues raised from shipping support shipping's decarbonisation, rather than simply increasing ETS and compliance costs without delivering additional emissions reductions," a Chamber spokesperson said in a statement on Thursday.

The explainer makes no mention of revenue for maritime decarbonisation.

title: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide
summary: The IMO's MEPC 85 convenes to address shipping's "net-zero divide," yet again facing "difficult negotiations" over proposed GHG reduction measures and the unresolved Net-Zero Framework. Despite the urgency, the agenda prioritizes theoretical technical and economic frameworks over immediate, tangible action to curb excessive HFO usage or improve abysmal CII ratings. Without swift, binding commitments, this latest MEPC risks being another forum for greenwashing, failing to impose real consequences on the industry's highest emitters.
content:
The International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) will convene in London from Nov 30-Dec 3 against a backdrop of intensifying pressure to deliver a landmark agreement on shipping decarbonisation, with delegates facing what many observers see as a defining moment for the sector’s climate transition.

The meeting follows a year of difficult negotiations over the organisation’s proposed mid-term greenhouse gas reduction measures.

While the committee’s agenda spans a broad range of environmental issues – including ballast water management, amendments to MARPOL and the NOx Technical Code, marine plastic litter, underwater radiated noise and maritime digitalisation – climate policy is expected to dominate proceedings.

Central to those discussions will be efforts to resolve outstanding differences over draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI and the package of mid-term measures envisioned under the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy.

According to the IMO, delegates will consider the outcomes of recent intersessional negotiations and seek ways to address “remaining concerns” surrounding the proposed measures, which combine technical and economic elements intended to accelerate emissions reductions from international shipping. The committee is also expected to continue work on the IMO’s Life Cycle GHG Assessment framework.

The significance of the discussions has been heightened by the unresolved fate of the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF), which environmental organisations argue is the industry’s best opportunity to establish a global mechanism for driving down emissions.

Adopt ‘as is’

The Clean Shipping Coalition (CSC), representing environmental non-governmental organisations engaged in IMO negotiations, has urged member states to finalise and adopt the framework before the end of the year.

“In order to fulfil the goals of the IMO’s GHG Strategy and to protect our global climate, the IMO and all its member states must adopt the Net-Zero Framework ‘as is’, without further diversion,” said Lukas Leppert, president of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.”

The coalition argues that the framework, originally approved during MEPC 83 in April 2025, already provides a balanced pathway for implementing the IMO’s decarbonisation objectives. The proposed package combines a global fuel standard with an economic mechanism designed to incentivise lower-carbon fuels and technologies. Adoption was delayed after opposition from a group of member states prevented final approval in October 2025.

Environmental groups contend that subsequent attempts to replace or significantly revise the framework have failed to attract broad support.

“Since October 2025, when IMO member states voted to adjourn the adoption session for one year, various alternative proposals to the NZF were introduced and intensively discussed, but were neither able to demonstrate a comparable reduction in emissions nor gather sufficient support,” Leppert said.

“These alternative proposals aimed at supplanting or distracting from the NZF have fallen away, proving the NZF as the best course ahead.”

The CSC frames MEPC 85 as a test of the IMO’s ability to convert years of negotiation into binding regulation. “There is no longer time for going in circles; every IMO member state must get behind the Net-Zero Framework and adopt it before the year ends,” Leppert said.

EU stance

Shipping industry representatives have also taken a view on how member states should proceed.

Ahead of the London meetings, Melina Travlos, president of the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS), warned that political divisions risk undermining efforts to secure a workable global solution. In a statement, she criticised the European Union’s negotiating stance and argued that flexibility remains essential if consensus is to be achieved.

“Two months after the inconclusive last round of negotiations at the IMO on reducing greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping, and with the next critical negotiating meetings approaching, there remains no evidence of positive tangible progress,” Travlos said.

She argued that recent discussions at European level had demonstrated an unwillingness to compromise, adding that

“the EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end, effectively torpedoing the negotiations by depriving them of the flexibility necessary for any chance of success.”

The Greek shipowners’ organisation has consistently advocated a global regulatory framework that recognises differing operational realities across shipping segments and trading patterns. Rather than focusing predominantly on alternative fuels, Travlos called for a broader approach incorporating operational and technical efficiency measures.

“For a regulation to be effective it must be pragmatic, proportionate and implementable, while reflecting the commercial and operational realities and constraints of the industry,” she said.

Travlos further argued that policymakers must align climate ambitions with technological readiness and fuel availability.

“This means taking into account the availability, scalability and affordability of alternative fuels, technologies and supporting infrastructure, as well as competing demand from other sectors,” she said. “Such a regulatory framework must also recognise the diversity of solutions available to the shipping industry, rather than focusing exclusively on alternative fuels. It should support all effective pathways to emissions reduction, including technical and operational efficiency measures.”

The contrasting positions highlight the challenge awaiting delegates in London. Environmental groups are pressing for rapid adoption of a framework they view as the culmination of years of climate negotiations, while shipowners and several member states are emphasising practicality, flexibility and the risks of imposing measures that outpace technology deployment and fuel availability.

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: The net-zero bargain
summary: The IMO's upcoming MEPC 85 faces critical decisions on a "net-zero" framework, yet significant pressure for compromise threatens to render any agreement ineffective against rising carbon intensity. Nations like Japan propose weaker fuel intensity targets, while the US actively opposes global emissions pricing, directly undermining efforts to curb shipping's environmental footprint. Such concessions will undoubtedly perpetuate reliance on high-carbon fuels and allow the dirtiest ships to continue polluting with minimal financial consequence under a façade of climate action.
content:
The IMO faces a difficult choice next month. A softer version of the Net-Zero Framework could help break the negotiating deadlock. But weaker rules could undermine the very transition it is meant to support.

The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) will reconvene from 30 November to 3 December to consider proposals ranging from stronger economic measures to removing greenhouse gas (GHG) pricing altogether.

Liberia, Tuvalu, Brazil and a four-country group comprising Australia, Canada, South Africa and the UK have submitted proposals for discussion at the IMO’s intersessional GHG working group meeting from 23 to 27 November.

Japan has submitted a proposal calling for softer fuel intensity targets and direct contributions, but it was not circulated within the six-month period required under MARPOL for adoption at MEPC 85.

The EU and Pacific Island states support adopting the text approved in April 2025. The US and several other countries, including major oil producers, want substantial changes to its technical and economic provisions.

US President Donald Trump has openly opposed global emissions pricing.

“There is no global government – and while I am President, there will be no global taxes,” he said.

The question is no longer simply whether governments can agree on a global framework, but whether the compromises needed to secure that agreement could leave shipping with rules too weak to drive meaningful change.

The case for compromise

The Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) has urged Brussels to show greater flexibility in negotiations.

“The EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end, effectively torpedoing the negotiations by depriving them of the flexibility necessary for any chance of success,” UGS president Melina Travlos said.

Travlos said Greece and three other EU member states, collectively representing 70% of the EU-controlled fleet, had pressed for the EU to approach the IMO talks with a genuine willingness to negotiate.

While she did not name the three countries supporting a compromise, Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy called for “realistic, globally applicable and cost effective” regulations during a ministerial meeting in Limassol in September. The four EU countries agreed to work towards the “widest possible consensus” on global measures that support shipping’s green fuel transition while keeping the sector competitive.

All four countries supported the framework’s approval in April 2025.

Nine shipping industry associations, including BIMCO, ICS, IBIA and WSC, have called for an “achievable, enforceable, and stable regulatory framework” that reflects fuel costs and availability.

“The regulatory framework must support credible transition pathways for existing ships and technologies. Continued industry investment and effective implementation will depend on global regulatory certainty and the reliable production and cost-competitiveness of alternative fuels at scale,” the statement said.

The associations also stressed the need to avoid overlapping regional and international requirements, including multiple charges on the same emissions. Travlos has made a similar argument, questioning whether the EU values its own regional measures, and the revenues they generate, more than a global agreement.

Charles Whitfield, chairman of Australian ammonia developer NH3 Clean Energy, expects IMO member states to reach an agreement in December, although he expects it to be less stringent than the April 2025 version.

“But I think that there will be a piece of paper or an agreement that does actually get ratified,” he told ENGINE.

Whitfield believes a common international framework would be preferable to the different regulatory approaches emerging across the EU, China and Singapore.

But at what cost?

Critics of a softer framework argue that political compromise could come at the expense of meaningful emissions reductions.

Weakening emissions targets or making compliance payments too cheap could undermine the IMO’s climate goals and slow the shift to cleaner marine fuels, according to a report by University College London’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group and the Rocky Mountain Institute.

The Clean Shipping Coalition has urged governments to adopt the framework without further changes. It argues that the existing text already represents years of negotiations and that alternative proposals have yet to demonstrate comparable emissions reductions or attract sufficient support.

The proposed IMO Net-Zero Fund is intended to support cleaner technologies, infrastructure and capacity-building, particularly in vulnerable countries. The availability of financial and technical support could help least developed and developing economies manage the transition.

Em Fenton, senior director of climate diplomacy at Opportunity Green, has cautioned against reopening the existing compromise.

“The Net-Zero Framework represents a hard-fought multilateral compromise. Any significant shift away from this text risks harming not only the level of emissions reductions that can be achieved from such a regulatory measure, but also the justice and equity of its implementation,” they told ENGINE.

“Further delay or weakening of the text only serves fossil fuel interests and does nothing to support climate vulnerable countries during shipping’s transition,” Fenton added.

A deal worth having?

Important questions remain unresolved, from lifecycle emissions accounting and chain of custody to GHG pricing and the proposed net-zero fund.

A weaker agreement could bring more governments on board and give shipping a common regulatory starting point. But if compliance becomes cheaper than switching fuels, that certainty may do little to encourage investment in cleaner alternatives.

In other alt fuels news this week, South Korea’s Lotte Fine Chemical and Norwegian shipping company Höegh Autoliners plan to expand green ammonia bunkering operations across South Korean ports.

Japanese shipping company NYK Line has unveiled a newbuild gas carrier equipped with an ammonia dual-fuel two-stroke main engine at Japan Marine United’s Ariake Shipyard in Kumamoto Prefecture.

title: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds
summary: Greek shipowners, with 5,800 vessels and 460 million DWT, face a staggering USD 78 billion in assets directly exposed to declining fossil fuel demand, particularly in oil and LNG carriers. This profound reliance on fossil fuel cargoes underscores mounting financial liabilities from delayed decarbonisation, including escalating carbon intensity fines under emerging regulations like FuelEU Maritime. Their push for a single IMO Net-Zero Framework appears less about genuine environmental ambition and more about self-preservation, seeking to manage predictable exits from their inherently dirty asset base.
content:
Greek shipowners hold around USD 78bn of assets exposed to the global energy transition, twice the exposure of Japan, the next most exposed ship owning nation. The risk relates to declining demand for fossil fuel cargoes which could reduce the need for vessels such as LNG carriers. It is separate but related to the risks faced by all shipowners as they manage the energy transition that will also take place within international shipping, whether driven by IMO regulation adopted this December, or postponed global regulation accompanied by a patchwork of regional regulation.

The new report finds that the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) is the most credible route to the single global rulebook that the shipping industry, including the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) has called for. A weaker, technical-only outcome at the IMO would leave the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) alongside the IMO fuel standard, as well as incentivising additions to other unilateral carbon pricing such as those already started in Africa – which is the regional patchwork UGS warns against.

Greece owns about a fifth of the world fleet, roughly 5,800 ships and 460 million deadweight tonnes (dwt). Greek shipowners collectively have particularly leading market shares in ownership of the oil tankers, LNG carriers and bulk carriers that move fossil fuels, making them more exposed to transition risks than any other nation. Owners cannot change demand for fossil fuel cargoes, but they can influence how shipping is regulated. The report finds that the NZF would give them a predictable timetable, more compliance options and a managed exit from LNG exposure, reducing the risk of stranded assets.

Dr Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport at UCL Energy Insitute and co-director of the Shipping and Oceans Research Group said “Greek owners already face one transition they cannot control, which is related to changes in the demand for the cargoes their ships carry. Supporting the NZF, the only adoptable architecture on the table at MEPC 85, is a chance to make the second one, in how shipping’s own energy transition is regulated, predictable, lower burden, less complicated and more supportive of a mix of decarbonisation strategies and pathways.”

The report, Real economy consequences for Greece from success or failure of the Net-Zero Framework, is published ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 (23 to 27 November) and MEPC 85, which opens on 30 November. At MEPC 84, NZF-like options drew more than twice the support of technical-only alternatives.

Earlier this week, UGS President Melina Travlos urged IMO member states to deliver a regulation that is “pragmatic, proportionate and implementable”, and questioned whether the EU is putting its regional measures, and the revenues they generate, ahead of a global deal. The report draws a similar concern about the risk of regulatory fragmentation, particularly how this could disadvantage smaller shipping companies with less capacity and flexibility to manage the administrative burden and timing of shipping’s energy transition. The report finds there is no alternative architecture to NZF that has anywhere close to the levels of support for adoption and efforts that do not support NZF are only increasing risks of stalemate and fragmentation. The European Commission’s commitment to avoid double payment depends on a global carbon price being adopted, so without one, the EU ETS would stay in force on top of the IMO standard.

Demetres Karavellas, CEO of WWF Greece said “As climate impacts intensify, shipping must play its part in the transition to net-zero. The IMO Net-Zero Framework is the only credible global pathway to decarbonise the sector while providing the certainty businesses need to invest. This report shows that Greece, as the world’s leading shipping nation, has more to lose from delay than almost anyone else. Opposing the NZF will not stop the transition. It will only increase uncertainty and expose Greek shipping to greater risk. Greece has an opportunity to help shape a global framework rather than face a more fragmented and disruptive transition later.”

The report concludes that failure to adopt the NZF, or a delay of more than a year, would weaken the IMO as global regulator, accelerate regional regulation and force a steeper decarbonisation pathway later. The report urges shipowners to engage constructively in developing the NZF and its guidelines, as the only viable, truly global framework.

Link to full report: https://www.shippingandoceans.com/post/greece-has-the-most-to-lose-from-delays-in-shipping-s-green-transition

Source: UCL Energy Institute

title: Get your data in order and set a course for greener shipping
summary: The shipping industry's self-proclaimed "green transition" is severely undermined by its acknowledged "data problem," conveniently hindering transparent reporting of actual vessel emissions. Without valid operational data, shipowners continue to rely on "uncertain and misleading" calculations, obscuring true carbon intensity and impeding genuine progress toward FuelEU Maritime compliance or meeting CII targets. This critical data deficit ensures that actual engine performance and excessive HFO usage remain opaque, perpetuating high emissions beyond reported CII ratings.
content:
There is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener. Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago. That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, which means shipowners are not getting the insights needed to accelerate the green transition.

In the coming weeks alone, there are two events worth keeping an eye on. From 23 to 27 November, the IMO’s working group known as ISWG-GHG 23 will continue its discussions on a global Net-Zero Framework – that is, proposals for common, global climate rules designed to steer the shipping industry towards net-zero emissions by 2050. A few days later, from 30 November to 3 December, the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) will convene for MEPC 85, with emissions, energy efficiency and environmental protection, amongst other topics, on the agenda.

There remains disagreement over the way forward, but the work being done within the IMO, amongst others, demonstrates a willingness to find common solutions. I sense the same willingness when I speak to shipping companies and other industry stakeholders. Compared with just three years ago, there is far greater interest in concrete climate action.

However, although progress is being made, the shipping industry still has a data problem. We still know too little about the emissions of individual ships and how they can reduce their fuel consumption. Far too many people still rely on calculations that are, at best, uncertain and, at worst, misleading.

Shipowners cannot navigate between new requirements and regulations blindfolded. They need valid data to set the right course. Calculations and standard values do not reveal how engines perform during operation or how high emissions really are.

In the coming years, shipping companies will have to deal with the use of multiple fuels, technologies and types of emissions. How do they assess emissions from different fuels whilst at sea? How do they demonstrate that an investment reduces emissions? And how do they determine the engine settings that deliver the lowest fuel consumption? Here, real-time measurements are a crucial tool – for documentation, compliance with requirements and day-to-day decision-making.

The new five-year partnership between the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Equinor is a strong example of how the green transition requires joint efforts and practical trials. They will collaborate on areas including alternative fuels, energy efficiency and CO₂ management. Their emphasis on documentation and verification is entirely appropriate.

After all, shipowners and organisations can only derive the full benefit from such initiatives if they have access to valid data. I therefore hope that they will involve experts in emissions measurement to a greater extent at an early stage of the process. This increases the likelihood that we can actually learn from each other’s experiences.

At the same time, shipowners can take advantage of some straightforward opportunities. Linking real-time measurements to the engines’ operational data would enable shipping companies to identify which operating conditions increase fuel consumption and emissions. However, without the necessary equipment on board, these opportunities are easily overlooked. With valid data, shipping companies can act immediately to reduce costs and cut emissions.

title: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization
summary: Major shipping lobby groups are predictably calling for global IMO regulations, framing it as a push for "decarbonization." This demand for "regulatory certainty" primarily serves to prevent regional measures like FuelEU Maritime from imposing immediate, higher costs and stricter carbon intensity limits. Their insistence on "achievable" and "stable" frameworks is a transparent attempt to control the pace of change, delaying tangible HFO reductions and avoiding genuine accountability for ships failing their CII ratings.
content:
In advance of the UN International Maritime Organization (IMO) Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), which meets in London from 30 November to 4 December 2026, this statement is made jointly by BIMCO, CLIA, IBIA, ICS, INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO, IPTA and WSC representing the global commercial shipping fleet.

The global shipping industry welcomes continuing efforts by all IMO Member States to agree on a global framework of practical, effective and fit for purpose regulations to help decarbonize international shipping and, whilst further improving energy efficiency, continue striving towards the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy goal of net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by or close to 2050.
