The industry recognizes that all proposals put forward by governments, and the elements these contain, remain under consideration, but emphasizes the importance of an achievable, enforceable, and stable regulatory framework which reflects cost and availability and provides clear incentives for the development and deployment of commercially viable alternative fuels. The regulatory framework must also meaningfully support a safe energy transition through solutions which are data-driven and fuel and technology neutral.

Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships, regardless of flag, ownership, trade or business model. A coordinated global approach at IMO must lead to the avoidance of regulatory fragmentation or regional or national measures which result in duplication of compliance requirements for ships or multiple charges for the same GHG emissions. During the transition to lower-GHG fuels, only global regulation can ensure a level playing field.

The GHG reduction regulations to be adopted by IMO Member States must reward verifiable emission reductions and incentivize, financially and/or technically, further investments that advance maritime decarbonization. In addition, the regulations should also provide optional/flexible compliance mechanisms so that shipping companies, large and small, can manage the transition, recognizing the current unavailability of commercially viable zero/near-zero GHG fuels and technologies (ZNZs) for the majority of the existing fleet.

The shipping industry has invested billions of dollars in new ships capable of using alternative low GHG fuels, innovative technologies, and fuel-flexible solutions. The regulatory framework must support credible transition pathways for existing ships and technologies. Continued industry investment and effective implementation will depend on global regulatory certainty and the reliable production and cost-competitiveness of alternative fuels at scale.

Shipowners and other maritime stakeholders, including marine fuel producers, charterers, ports and financiers, all need investment certainty to support the maritime energy transition. An effective global regulatory framework agreed at the IMO is essential to provide clear predictable production pathways for further emissions reductions. To drive decarbonization across the shipping industry, support fleet renewal and financing decisions and maintain a global level playing field, the framework must be pragmatic, fit for purpose and underpinned by clear and enforceable obligations. This framework needs to be agreed as soon as practicable by the industry’s global regulator, the IMO.

Achieving an agreement at IMO will require constructive engagement by all Member States, on all sides of the debate, with the full range of alternative proposals on the table, to identify areas of convergence and to draw on their most effective elements, so as to develop a global solution that takes into account strategic ambition as well as market and technological readiness.

title: Shipping Industry Presses for Global IMO Climate Deal as Divisions Over Rules Persist
summary: Nine major shipping associations are demanding a global IMO climate deal, claiming regulatory uncertainty hinders investment in cleaner ships and alternative fuels. However, their insistence on "flexible compliance mechanisms" and avoiding regional regulations appears designed to dilute effective decarbonization efforts. While industry lobbies for a global framework, the continued reliance on heavy fuel oil and excessive carbon intensity from many vessels remains largely unaddressed by these proposals.
content:
Nine major shipping associations are urging governments to reach an agreement on global greenhouse gas regulations, warning that continued uncertainty threatens investment in cleaner ships and alternative fuels ahead of critical negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

The joint statement, issued Wednesday, calls for practical, enforceable and globally consistent rules that would give shipowners and fuel suppliers the certainty needed to invest in maritime decarbonization.

The appeal comes as governments prepare to revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, whose formal adoption was postponed in October 2025 amid opposition from the United States and several oil-producing countries.

The framework, approved in draft form in April 2025, would combine progressively stricter greenhouse gas fuel-intensity requirements with a mechanism that places a price on certain emissions.

The nine organizations—including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERTANKO, INTERCARGO and the World Shipping Council (WSC)—reaffirmed their support for the IMO’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050.

However, they stressed that any agreement must account for the cost and availability of alternative fuels, provide flexible compliance mechanisms and avoid overlapping national and regional regulations.

The statement stops short of explicitly endorsing the existing Net-Zero Framework in its current form, instead acknowledging that alternative government proposals remain under consideration.

Industry Support Comes With Conditions

The appeal follows a recent analysis by InfluenceMap that found broad industry support for a global IMO climate agreement, but significant differences over carbon pricing, fuel standards and how emissions from alternative fuels should be calculated.

The London-based research organization found that industry support has become more cautious since the framework’s adoption was postponed last year.

Before that decision, ICS and WSC had backed the proposed framework as is. More recently, shipping associations have emphasized reaching an agreement without explicitly endorsing the original package.

Another point of contention is the relationship between global IMO rules and existing European regulations. Several shipping associations have called for reviewing or harmonizing the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime requirements once an international framework is established, arguing that overlapping regulations would impose unnecessary costs.

Critical Negotiations Ahead

The renewed industry push comes ahead of an IMO working group meeting November 23–27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s MEPC 85 session from November 30 to December 3. A previously adjourned extraordinary session could resume December 4 to consider adoption of the framework.

Negotiators face deep divisions over carbon pricing, compliance costs and the treatment of different marine fuels.

For shipowners making investment decisions on vessels expected to operate for decades, the outcome could shape everything from ship design to fuel procurement and infrastructure development.

The industry groups say a global agreement is essential to maintaining a level playing field. Whether governments can deliver that certainty while preserving the emissions-reduction ambitions of the original framework remains an open question.

title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
summary: Nine major shipping associations are lobbying the IMO for a single global carbon pricing mechanism, claiming regional regulations create "double charges." This industry-led push prioritizes financial predictability and minimizing compliance costs over accelerating genuine decarbonization efforts. Operators must still be held accountable for excessive carbon intensity and continued high-volume HFO usage, irrespective of a unified regulatory landscape.
content:
Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions.

The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) later this month, with governments still divided over how to regulate and price shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions.

BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Intercargo, Intertanko, the World Shipping Council, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), Interferry, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and the International Parcel Tankers Association (IPTA) have called for a single global framework that applies equally to vessels regardless of flag, ownership or trade.

“Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships,” the organisations said.

The groups warned that national and regional schemes could result in duplicated compliance requirements and multiple charges for the same emissions, undermining efforts to establish a level playing field.

They want an IMO agreement that rewards verifiable emissions reductions while giving shipowners sufficient flexibility to manage the transition to cleaner fuels, many of which remain commercially unavailable for much of the existing fleet.

The joint statement also calls for regulations that are fuel- and technology-neutral, enforceable and backed by clear incentives for investment in alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies.

The intervention comes after the IMO failed to secure agreement on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in October 2025, forcing governments to postpone adoption for a year.

The framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism, remains the subject of negotiations over its cost, design and implementation.

The industry’s latest appeal follows growing concern over the spread of regional carbon schemes. Several African governments are moving towards their own shipping emissions charges, while European operators already face the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations.

The nine associations warned that the lack of regulatory certainty is complicating investment decisions for shipowners, ports, fuel producers and financiers, particularly given the limited availability and high cost of lower-emissions fuels.

Governments will resume negotiations at the IMO’s greenhouse gas working group from November 23 to 27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3.

A further extraordinary session to consider adoption of the emissions framework could take place on December 4, subject to confirmation during MEPC 85.

title: Nine global shipping associations urge IMO to adopt unified maritime emissions framework – Chamber of Shipping
summary: Nine major shipping associations, including ICS and WSC, are now demanding a "unified global framework" for maritime emissions, following the IMO's postponed net-zero framework. Their primary concern appears to be avoiding "duplicate carbon charges" and multiple compliance requirements, rather than accelerating genuine decarbonization efforts. This industry-led push for "flexibility" and "fuel-neutrality" will only further delay concrete action on carbon intensity and excessive HFO use.
content: Nine leading international shipping associations, including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping, Intercargo, Intertanko and the World Shipping Council, have jointly called for a unified global framework to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping. Ahead of upcoming International Maritime Organization (IMO) negotiations, the associations warned that fragmented national and regional regulations could create duplicate compliance requirements and multiple carbon charges for the same emissions. They emphasized the need for fuel- and technology-neutral regulations, consistent enforcement, incentives for emissions reductions and flexibility for shipowners transitioning to alternative fuels. The appeal follows the postponement of the IMO Net-Zero Framework in October 2025 amid disagreements over its proposed fuel standards and emissions-pricing mechanisms. Negotiations are scheduled to resume from November 23–27, followed by MEPC 85 from November 30 to December 3, with potential consideration of the framework’s adoption on December 4.

title: Critics say methane plumes at Chevron's Gorgon LNG project expose gaps in greenhouse gas monitoring
summary: Massive methane plumes detected by satellite at Chevron's Gorgon LNG facility expose severe deficiencies in Australia's greenhouse gas monitoring and reporting. Regulators were slow to respond to the UN alert, while emissions are often estimated by formula, not direct measurement. This systemic underreporting compromises the foundational data for carbon intensity metrics and FuelEU Maritime compliance throughout the entire shipping supply chain.
content:
Observers are warning that massive methane plumes detected at one of Australia's biggest oil and gas projects are symptoms of a much larger problem.

Clouds of the greenhouse gas were picked up by five consecutive satellite passes over Chevron's Gorgon LNG facility off Barrow Island in Western Australia's Pilbara.

It triggered a formal alert to Chevron in late August by the United Nations Environment Programme.

But WA's Department of Water and Environment Regulation (DWER) says it did not become aware of the notification until September 28.

A spokesperson initially said the department was still trying to "understand what compliance or regulatory measures may be required", before confirming an investigation some days later.

Energy analyst Kevin Morrison, from the Institute of Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), said the response was "telling".

"Had this not been picked up on the satellite data, it's very unlikely it would have been recorded in any official emissions statistics," he said.

Safeguard shortcomings

The methane emissions sparked a protest outside Chevron's Perth offices on Monday, with the WA Greens calling the state's emissions monitoring regime "broken".

Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn told WA Parliament this week the matter remained under investigation, and that Chevron had advised DWER there were no on-site incidents on the day of the August detection at Gorgon.

While day-to-day monitoring is the responsibility of the state, operators like Chevron must record their emissions annually under the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting (NGER) scheme.

Rather than using instrument measurements, however, the output is calculated with a formula set by the federal Climate Change Regulator.

"It's done on an estimation, based on a sum, an algorithm," Mr Morrison said.

"The numbers we get are not a true reflection of what's been actually pumped up into the atmosphere."

Mr Morrison said the process — even when tailored to the specifics of a project — vastly under-reports the fugitive emissions that escape during LNG production.

He added the incident at Chevron was just the tip of the iceberg, with methane emissions across Australia's gas and coal sectors more than doubling the official estimates.

Mr Morrison also questioned the credits administered under the Commonwealth's Safeguard Mechanism, which could be purchased by companies to ensure they were hitting legislated targets.

Gorgon surrendered 478,000 credits to meet its safeguard baseline at the end of the last financial year, having notched 8.76 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions and 252,000 tonnes of methane emissions.

Mr Morrison said buying credits was not the same as making genuine reductions.

"The Safeguard Mechanism is a get-out-of-jail card … companies can pretend that they've lowered their emissions by buying these offsets," he said.

Regulator backs scheme

A 2023 review of the reporting scheme concluded it was performing well despite posing 25 recommendations for improvement.

"The government has amended the NGER scheme to enhance the accuracy and transparency of reported fugitive methane emissions," a spokesperson for the federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment, and Water (DCCEEW) said.

"In April this year, this data reported that total methane emissions from all Safeguard facilities are equivalent to 22.7 million tonnes, down from 23.1 million tonnes the year before."

Chevron said it continued to work with authorities, including DWER, and provide information as required.

"We take our environmental obligations seriously and are committed to managing emissions from our operations in accordance with relevant regulatory requirements," the company said.

Satellite monitoring

A 2026 interim report by a Fugitive Methane Expert Panel appointed by Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen found satellites should play a more central role in identifying anomaly events, such as leaks, by major emitters.

While Australia helps fund networks like the UN's International Methane Emissions Observatory, of which Chevron is also a partner, these alerts are non-binding and information sharing between federal and state regulators is limited.

Chevron played down the effectiveness of space-borne monitoring in previous statements to the ABC.

"Satellite observations capture a single moment in time and have a wide range of uncertainty," the spokesperson said.

Last month, researchers published a year-long blind test of methane observations by satellite and found Tanager-1, responsible for the detections at Chevron's Gorgon plant, never missed emissions or triggered a false positive.

Co-author and professor of energy science engineering at Stanford University Adam Brandt said the Gorgon observations were worthy of public confidence.

Dr Brandt noted the satellite, operated by non-profit Carbon Mapper, was "quite conservative" and "best-in-class".

"With five separate detections, the chance that they are seeing something that doesn't exist is extremely small," he said.

"This is almost certainly a real plume."

title: Sustainable Shipping Initiative and partners target ‘blue shipping corridors’ to harmonise shipping decarbonisation with better ocean health
summary: The Sustainable Shipping Initiative (SSI) and over 35 partners are now pushing for 'blue shipping corridors,' a conceptual expansion of 'green corridors' to integrate 'ocean health' with decarbonisation talks. This COP31 'Ambition Statement' outlines a vision for zero-emission routes and marine conservation, yet primarily focuses on 'enabling environments' and annual progress reviews, rather than concrete regulation. While the rhetoric includes 'nature-positive port design' and 'smarter routing,' it offers little immediate impact on the carbon intensity of today's global fleet or the persistent usage of heavy fuel oil.
content:
The Sustainable Shipping Initiative (SSI) has called on governments to help establish ‘blue shipping corridors’, extending the role of green corridors, established to accelerate decarbonisation in key shipping lanes, to include ocean health. SSI is co-leading the statement through the Marine Biodiversity and Ocean Health Breakthrough, the initiative that started this process, and identified that decarbonisation and ocean health are two sides of the same coin.

The statement, COP31 Blue Shipping Corridors Ambition Statement, is backed by more than 35 organisations from across shipping, ports, finance, science and conservation, including WWF, World Resources Institute, the UN Global Compact, Ocean Conservancy, IFAW, Lloyd’s Register Foundation, Transport & Environment, Jotun, Plymouth Marine Laboratory and GRID-Arendal. Together they are making the case that green corridors for ships, which are dedicated maritime trade routes where zero-emission and low-carbon shipping is developed, can do the same for ocean conservation, marine life and coastal communities. Green corridors have become one of shipping’s most practical tools for convening first movers, fuel suppliers, ports and cargo owners around shared decarbonisation decisions on a defined route.

The new Ambition Statement, drafted by the Marrakech Partnership Maritime Stakeholders, sets out a vision for corridors that enable zero- or near-zero-emission shipping, deliver significant ocean conservation measures at sea and in port with a net positive impact on ocean health and marine biodiversity, and bring real benefits to coastal communities without harming biodiversity on land. Endorsers commit to working towards an enabling environment that covers everything from nature-positive port design and smarter routing to better ocean data, a skilled workforce, a just transition for remote and underserved ports, and an annual review of progress.

Many of the solutions dovetail, offering dual benefits to the climate and the oceans. For example, International Maritime Organisation (IMO) research found that a layer of slime as thin as 0.5mm covering up to half a hull can push GHG emissions up by 20–25%, while the same fouling carries invasive species into new seas. A clean hull cuts fuel bills, emissions and the spread of invaders in one go. In the same way, slowing ships in hotspots not only reduces underwater noise, emissions and air pollution for coastal communities, it also prevents collisions with whales.

Today’s announcement builds upon SSI’s Shipping and Ocean Health 2026 Report which shows that the actions that decarbonise shipping can often protect the seas at little or no additional cost. However, progress has been held back by access to finance, cross-sector collaboration and a clear business case, all of which blue corridors are well placed to help overcome.

Ellie Besley-Gould, Chief Executive Officer, Sustainable Shipping Initiative, said: “Green corridors have shown what’s possible when shipowners, ports, fuel suppliers and governments commit to a route together. Blue shipping corridors take that model and recognise that if we’re already rethinking these routes from the ground up, it makes complete sense to make them better for the ocean at the same time. So many of the measures that cut emissions, like cleaner hulls and slower, smarter voyages, also take pressure off marine life, often at little or no extra cost. It would be a real missed opportunity not to capture those wins. The industry is ready to step up and earnestly support action in this space. What we need now is for governments to put the conditions in place so it can.”

title: UK Moves Toward New Maritime Fuel Standard
summary: The UK's Department for Transport is consulting on a "new" maritime fuel standard for 2030, suspiciously mirroring the EU's FuelEU Maritime for ships over 5,000 GT. Despite claims of emissions reduction, the proposed "flexibility mechanisms"—pooling, banking, and borrowing—offer familiar loopholes for avoiding tangible decarbonization. With implementation a distant 2030 and key emission reduction targets still undefined, this 'consultation' offers little immediate assurance against excessive carbon intensity or HFO usage.
content:
The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of their fuels beginning in 2030.

The Department for Transport’s proposal, published Monday, November 16, would establish a fuel standard broadly aligned with the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation while leaving room for adjustments as international negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) continue.

Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, regardless of flag, covering approximately 5,000 vessels based on historical port-call data.

The proposed framework would regulate all energy used on domestic voyages between UK ports, 50% of energy used on international voyages to and from the UK, and energy consumed by covered ships while at berth in British ports.

Rather than mandating particular fuels, the regulation would establish progressively tightening limits on the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity of energy consumed by ships. Operators could meet those requirements through alternative fuels, electrification and other lower-emission energy sources.

The government is also considering compliance flexibility mechanisms, including pooling, banking and borrowing emissions credits, similar to provisions under FuelEU Maritime.

However, several important details remain undecided, including how quickly emissions limits would tighten and whether the UK should follow the EU’s trajectory, align with future IMO standards or establish its own targets.

The government expects the regulation to take effect from 2030.

Industry Welcomes Consultation, Warns of Practical Challenges

The UK Chamber of Shipping welcomed the consultation but urged policymakers to ensure that new requirements reflect the availability of alternative fuels, supporting infrastructure and commercially viable technologies.

“We welcome the Government moving forward with this consultation. Greater long-term certainty can help unlock the investment needed to decarbonise shipping, but regulation needs to develop alongside the fuels, infrastructure and technology that operators will need,” a Chamber spokesperson said.

“Any future UK framework must be practical, support investment and maintain the international competitiveness of UK shipping.”

The Chamber has previously called for a regulatory framework that avoids duplicating existing international requirements while providing operators with sufficient flexibility to manage the transition.

In an October policy paper, the organization recommended aligning fuel certification and lifecycle emissions accounting with emerging IMO standards, developing reliable monitoring and verification systems, and setting targets based on realistic assessments of fuel availability and infrastructure readiness.

Those concerns are particularly relevant given the significant overlap between ships trading to the UK and those already subject to European regulations.

According to the government’s consultation, approximately 97% of ships above 5,000 gross tonnage that called at UK ports in 2019 also called at EU ports.

UK Presses Ahead Amid IMO Uncertainty

The consultation comes as the international shipping industry continues to grapple with uncertainty surrounding the IMO’s proposed global Net-Zero Framework.

While the UK government acknowledges that international regulation remains the most effective way to reduce shipping emissions, it argues that uncertainty over global measures should not prevent domestic action.

The proposed fuel regulation would complement the UK’s existing maritime carbon-pricing measures, including the extension of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to domestic shipping in July 2026.

The government is also seeking industry feedback on whether smaller ships should eventually be included, with vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnage remaining under review.

Beyond the emissions requirements themselves, the consultation examines the availability of alternative maritime fuels, bunkering infrastructure, port readiness and the investment needed to support widespread adoption.

The Department for Transport has emphasized that its proposals are preliminary and that no final regulatory decisions have been made.

The consultation remains open until February 22, 2027.

The UK Chamber of Shipping said it will work with its members and the UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition to develop a detailed response addressing the operational, commercial and technical implications of the proposed framework.

title: New US Policy Priorities Could Shape Future Shipping Markets
summary: US policy shifts, potentially easing tensions around Hormuz, are seen by shipbrokers primarily as a catalyst for increased tanker demand and lower energy prices. This market-centric outlook entirely neglects the environmental cost, as more vessels will likely burn heavy fuel oil (HFO) without explicit decarbonization mandates. Geopolitical stability must integrate urgent carbon intensity targets and FuelEU Maritime compliance, rather than merely facilitating cheaper, dirtier transport.
content:
A potential shift in US policy guidance could trigger new catalysts for the global shipping markets in the years to come. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “the Democratic Party’s victory in the US midterm elections, securing control of both chambers of Congress from January 2027, is expected to influence Washington’s foreign, energy, trade and maritime policies. Democrats will gain greater leverage over legislation, government spending and congressional oversight. Beyond these institutional powers, the election outcome itself could prompt President Trump to reassess certain policy priorities, even without direct Democratic pressure, as the administration considers the political and economic implications of the result. Nevertheless, Trump retains substantial executive authority, and the extent of any policy adjustments remains uncertain”.

According to Mr. Nikos Tagoulis, Head of Research Department with Intermodal, “among the issues with the most immediate implications for shipping is the conflict involving Iran. Democrats are expected to intensify pressure for diplomatic de-escalation and greater congressional oversight of military operations, potentially supporting efforts to restore safe navigation through Hormuz. However, ending military operations, securing maritime passage and adjusting sanctions on Iranian petroleum remain separate policy decisions, with progress dependent on negotiations between Washington and Tehran”.

“Any sustained improvement in maritime security around Hormuz could have significant implications for energy and commodity trade. A reopening of the Strait could facilitate the recovery of Middle Eastern exports, easing energy prices, war-risk premiums and transportation costs. Qatar’s LNG exports could gradually recover, although the extent and timing of production restoration remain uncertain following Iranian strikes on liquefaction infrastructure. A recovery in cargo volumes could support tanker demand, while the normalization of trading patterns and vessel availability could moderate exceptionally high freight rates and reduce ton mile demand. For dry bulk, some of the most notable market effects could include a recovery in regional fertilizer exports, while the resumption of LNG exports and lower gas prices could reduce gas-to-coal switching and thermal coal imports in some markets, potentially weighing on thermal coal trade”, Mr. Tagoulis said.

“Black Sea represents another area of interest for shipping. Democrats have prioritized increased assistance to Ukraine, although greater congressional support would not necessarily accelerate a ceasefire, with any lasting settlement dependent on developments between Russia and Ukraine. For shipowners, the restoration of reliable commercial navigation, port operations and export corridors would remain central to any agreement”, he added.

According to Mr. Tagoulis, “beyond these geopolitical developments, the Democratic victory could influence US trade policy, with Democrats potentially favouring more selective tariffs, closer cooperation with traditional allies and targeted measures supporting strategic US industries, rather than the broad-based tariffs introduced under President Trump. In the maritime sector, the suspension of US port fees affecting Chinese-built and Chinese-linked vessels has been extended until 10 January 2027, shortly after the new Democratic Congress takes office, potentially prompting early congressional scrutiny of its scope and implementation, although final decisions remain with the administration. Furthermore, maritime decarbonization represents another area where Democratic influence could become more pronounced. Democrats generally favour cleaner energy and stronger international environmental cooperation and could advocate renewed US engagement with the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, while also promoting greater investment in alternative marine fuels, lower-emission vessels and greener shipping practices”.

“These environmental priorities could also shape domestic US energy policy, with potential consequences for seaborne energy trade. Democrats may seek to expand renewable energy while advocating greater environmental scrutiny of future offshore oil exploration and new LNG export authorizations, potentially influencing the longer-term outlook for US fossil-fuel production and exports. Meanwhile, the Jones Act and efforts to revitalize domestic shipbuilding appear to retain bipartisan support, suggesting greater continuity in US maritime industrial policy. With the current Jones Act waiver due to expire on 15 November, attention could also turn to the potential extension of exemptions”, Tagoulis noted.

title: Onboard carbon capture: a practical pathway for shipping?
summary: The shipping industry's glacial pace in adopting alternative fuels means fossil fuel dependency, and thus high emissions, will persist for years, with orders for alternative-fuel-capable vessels declining. Onboard Carbon Capture (oCCS) is emerging as a supposed solution, with systems like those on the Pacific Cobalt capturing 30-40% of CO2. However, this technology demands a 15-30% increase in fuel consumption to operate, raising serious questions about actual net emissions reduction, FuelEU Maritime compliance, and continued HFO reliance.
content:
Many ships carrying global trade today will be operating well into the 2030s, yet the transition to alternative fuels takes time. Of the near-zero emission fuel production capacity estimated to be needed by 2030 only around 4% has reached a final investment decision. Worse, alternative-fuel-capable vessel orders fell from 45% of contracted tonnage in 2024 to 37% in 2025.

This means the global fleet will remain dependent on fossil fuels, or their bio- or e- equivalents, for years to come and must find novel ways to reduce emissions. Energy-efficiency measures reduce fuel consumption, but even those more efficient crossings will continue to produce carbon emissions.

A potential role opens for onboard carbon capture and storage (oCCS). By capturing CO₂ from engine exhausts before it reaches the atmosphere, oCCS could help vessels that cannot yet switch to zero- or near-zero emission fuels drastically reduce their emissions.

From first installations to commercial use

Early commercial installations show oCCS moving beyond concept and pilot-scale development, with amine-based post-combustion capture emerging as the most mature marine option. This is currently the only technology with classed commercial installations, where full-scale systems capture around 30% to 40% of CO₂ emissions. Larger pilots target about 70%.

Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Pacific Cobalt became the first classed commercial oCCS installation in 2024 under LR’s Emission Abatement Carbon Capture & Storage (EACCS) (Amine, HFO) class notation, while Solvang’s Clipper Eris is testing a full-scale system designed to capture around 70% of the CO₂ produced by its main engine. These projects add to the growing evidence that oCCS can operate at commercial scale, but its wider value depends on the emissions reductions achieved in practice.

That depends partly on the energy needed to operate the system, which can increase fuel consumption by 15% to 30% in current applications. A 70% gross capture with a 15% fuel penalty would deliver an estimated tank-to-wake CO₂ reduction of around 44%, although waste-heat recovery could reduce that penalty. The resulting emissions reduction, cost and operational impact will vary between ships, making vessel suitability central to the business case.

Finding the right ships

Panos Mitrou, LR Senior Vice President of Shipping Strategy states: “Onboard carbon capture has the potential to become an important part of shipping’s decarbonisation toolkit. For the right vessel types and trades, it offers a realistic pathway to reducing CO₂ emissions and managing carbon costs while fuel supply chains, infrastructure and regulations continue to evolve.”

The strongest opportunities for oCCS are likely to be those vessels with sufficient remaining trading life and space for the equipment. The business case will also depend on how and where these vessels operate. For example, medium range and chemical tankers trading on EEA routes have frequent port calls, offering opportunities to offload captured CO₂ while EU carbon-price exposure increases the value of reducing emissions.

For LNG-fuelled vessels and LNG carriers, cold energy released during LNG vaporisation can help liquefy captured CO₂, reducing additional power requirements. Short-sea and feeder vessels could also benefit from predictable routes and regular opportunities to offload. The case for oCCS therefore depends on the technology fitting a vessel’s operating and commercial conditions.

Without these or similar conditions, the case weakens. Ships with limited trading life, little carbon-price exposure or poor access to offloading facilities will be less likely to justify the investment. Access to offloading is another critical factor because onboard storage is limited, setting a limit on how long the system can operate before captured CO₂ must be removed. Voyage length and offloading opportunities therefore directly affect how much CO₂ can ultimately be captured, making where and how a vessel operates as important as what can be installed onboard.

The decisive challenge lies ashore

For oCCS to deliver its intended benefits, captured CO₂ must enter a transport and storage network leading to permanent storage or an eligible use. Limited port reception infrastructure is a constraint, with few ports able to receive ship-captured liquefied CO₂. Many existing facilities are designed for food-grade CO₂ that may not suit exhaust-derived streams. Development is furthest ahead in north-west Europe, supported by emerging North Sea transport and storage networks, but access remains limited elsewhere.

The emissions benefit must also be recognised within relevant regulatory frameworks. The EU ETS can recognise captured CO₂ that reaches qualifying permanent storage or utilisation, while FuelEU Maritime does not yet include oCCS in its greenhouse-gas intensity calculations. The IMO is still developing a global framework covering safety, testing, verification and carbon accounting. Practically, the success of oCCS depends on infrastructure and regulation developing alongside the technology.

Entering an oCCS world

oCCS could offer an emissions-reduction pathway for suitable vessels using fossil fuels or their artificial equivalents as the transition to zero and near-zero emission fuels develops. But there are constraints.

Success depends on matching effective capture technology to ships with enough trading life remaining and suitable trading patterns, to form a strong commercial case. Regular offloading access and supporting transport and storage infrastructure must be developed to connect captured CO₂ to permanent storage or an eligible use. Regulation also needs to recognise the resulting emissions reduction, to help create a working carbon economy.

Where these technical, operational, commercial, infrastructure and regulatory conditions align, oCCS could help bridge the gap between a carbon-intensive present and a carbon-neutral future.

title: Brønnbåt Nord Well-Boat to Run on Everllence 175D Variable-Speed GenSets
summary: Brønnbåt Nord's new well-boat will deploy Everllence 175D variable-speed GenSets, with the manufacturer touting "state-of-the-art hybrid-propulsion" and "industry-leading fuel-oil consumption." While the engines are marketed as "extremely eco-friendly" and "cleared for operation on biofuels," the announcement provides no commitment to actual biofuel use or quantified CO2 reductions upon delivery. Without transparent data on projected carbon intensity or immediate low-carbon fuel adoption, this remains typical greenwashing rhetoric, obscuring the vessel's real environmental footprint for FuelEU Maritime compliance.
content:
The new vessel is a further development of Brønnbåt Nord’s Caspian, a 2,800 m³ well-boat that was delivered in 2024 and that also features an Everllence engine setup with one 8L27/38 propulsion engine and one 12V175D GenSet.

Ruben Fernandez—Head of High-Speed, Four-Stroke Marine, Everllence—said: “Winning a follow-up order to the Caspian underlines the owner’s continued confidence in the performance, reliability and efficiency of the 175D platform. This new vessel has state-of-the-art hybrid-propulsion technology where the 175D variable-speed GenSets have industry-leading fuel-oil and lube-oil consumption values in their power range. Combined with its reliability and high energy density, the 175D is the perfect fit for demanding fishing and aquaculture applications.”

Everllence’s scope of supply for the newbuild well-boat also includes permanent-magnet (PM) alternators. With a smaller footprint than standard asynchronous alternators, these combine a compact, lightweight design with high efficiency across a broad operating-speed range that makes them particularly well-suited to variable-speed GenSets. Furthermore, they maximize overall system efficiency, thereby reducing fuel consumption.

About Everllence’s 175D Engine

Everllence developed the 175D engine range to supplement and complete its product portfolio in the maritime sector. In three variants of 12-, 16-, and 20-cylinders, the engine is available with an output ranging from 1,440 to 4,400 kW and is optimized for propelling offshore support ships, tugs, and sundry working vessels. Other, demanding applications like superyachts and the navy also rely on 175D power delivery.

The 175D is an extremely eco-friendly engine and is designed to minimize operational costs, having been designed from the outset for low fuel consumption. This is coupled with compliance with the latest exhaust-gas-emission standards while also considering future-fuel requirements, as it is already cleared for operation on biofuels such as FAME and HVO.

It is also delivered as methanol-ready for later conversion to methanol operation if required. Additionally, Everllence recently announced the 175DF-M, a high-speed, dual-fuel variant designed to operate on both diesel and methanol from the outset, with first customer deliveries planned for 2027.

title: Greek shipowners put Brussels on the spot over IMO deadlock
summary: Greek shipowners sharply criticize the EU for prioritizing its regional carbon regulations and associated revenue over a critical global IMO emissions agreement. This political deadlock risks stalling meaningful progress on carbon intensity, allowing high-emitting vessels to operate without robust international oversight. While policymakers squabble, the industry's dirtiest ships continue to burn fossil fuels, unhindered by effective, unified global standards.
content:
Greek shipowners have launched a fresh attack on Brussels ahead of the next round of international shipping emissions negotiations, accusing the European Union of putting its own regulatory interests ahead of a global agreement.

Union of Greek Shipowners president Melina Travlos warned on Monday that the EU’s unwillingness to compromise risks pushing the International Maritime Organization into another deadlock when talks resume in London next week.

Travlos said there had been no meaningful progress since the previous negotiating round in September and questioned whether Brussels was more interested in preserving its regional carbon regulations and the revenue they generate than securing a worldwide deal.

Greece and three other EU member states, together controlling around 70% of Europe’s shipping fleet according to Travlos, have repeatedly called for greater flexibility in the European negotiating position.

Those appeals, she said, had gone unanswered.

The intervention comes ahead of a November 23–27 IMO working group meeting, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3. A further extraordinary session has been scheduled provisionally for December 4, subject to confirmation.

The talks will revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism. The negotiations have been held up by disagreements over the design, cost and implementation of the measures.

Travlos called for a framework reflecting the availability and cost of alternative fuels, the readiness of supporting infrastructure and competition for new fuels from other industries.

She also argued that energy-efficiency improvements and operational measures must remain part of the emissions-reduction toolkit rather than placing almost all the emphasis on alternative fuels.

Greek owners have long favoured a single international regulatory regime over overlapping regional requirements. The latest statement sharpens that position by directly questioning the EU’s negotiating intentions just days before governments return to London.

title: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost
summary: The IMO's "net-zero" framework faces critical delays, with member states failing to agree on crucial financial penalties for excessive emissions. The US leads opposition to a global carbon tax, effectively gutting incentives for shipping lines to abandon cheap, high-carbon fuels. Without mandatory financial consequences, claims of "decarbonization" remain mere greenwashing, as operators will predictably avoid more expensive, cleaner alternatives.
content:
Countries are struggling to design rules to make shipping companies comply with a new bunker regulation designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a senior International Bunker Industry Association official said Nov. 12, as Washington leads opposition to financial punitive measures.

International Maritime Organization member states, having failed to adopt the Net-Zero Framework as scheduled in October 2025, are due to meet again between Nov. 23 and Dec. 4 to discuss the regulation.

“People recognize that we need a GHG intensity marine fuel standard, and that is sort of generally agreed,” Edmund Hughes, IBIA’s representative to the UN agency, told Platts. “The sticking point is on the financial aspects.”

In its current form, the framework is composed of GHG intensity thresholds for marine energy that tighten progressively over 2028-2035, and financial costs for shipping companies failing to meet the standards.

But the US has fiercely opposed what it describes as “a global carbon tax” on shipping for the financial element, and a growing number of member states have proposed various revisions to the framework in bids to achieve a compromise.

“That is where we have the trouble. Because, obviously, the member states haven’t been able to identify the best approach,” Hughes said on the sidelines of the IBIA Annual Convention 2026.

Compliance mechanism

Countries supporting the current net-zero framework have designed the financial element to promote the use of low-carbon marine fuels, which remain much more costly than conventional, oil-based fuels due to limited availability.

October’s average delivered bunker costs for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil are $22.78 per gigajoule in Singapore, compared with $27/GJ for bioblend B24, $28.48/GJ for LNG, and $48.47/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator.

“No shipping company is going to carry on buying more expensive fuel while their competitors are not,” Hughes said. “You need some way of closing that price gap.”

The IBIA official said challenges lie ahead for member states on how to design an alternative compliance mechanism if the current net-zero framework is to be revised.

Most Pacific Island states and EU member states are officially still supporting the current net-zero framework while the US and Middle Eastern states remain opposed to it. Japan, China, Norway and some major flag states have presented new ideas on compliance mechanisms.

“If you have a technical standard, you have to find a way to comply with it,” Hughes said. “You can go through quite a few semantic gymnastics to try and get the agreement, and that’s often what’s done at international level in multilateral discussions.”

Outlook

IBIA, the world’s largest trade association representing bunker industry participants, including bunker traders and fuel suppliers, has been granted consultative status with the IMO and its representatives regularly participate in IMO meetings.

“We recognize and value, as a sector, having global rules,” Hughes said. “That helps in all sorts of aspects in terms of understanding what the compliance requirements are, understanding what the market needs, what we need to provide in terms of fuels, and what people want to buy.”

Going forward, Hughes said IMO member states may need to coalesce around a net-zero framework in a return to its tradition of consensus building so future implementation could be ensured globally.

In April 2025, a total of 63 countries won a vote to approve the framework’s current text after the US withdrew from the negotiations. Later, 57 countries won another vote to delay its adoption in October 2025.

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: A drop in the tank
summary: Despite "alternative" fuel announcements, current small-scale projects offer negligible volumes against shipping's immense demand. Facilities producing just 1,000 to 10,000 tonnes of e-methanol annually represent mere drops compared to the thousands of tonnes a single vessel consumes. This insufficient progress guarantees continued reliance on high-carbon HFO, making FuelEU Maritime compliance and improved carbon intensity ratings an industry-wide challenge.
content:
Several producers are developing small-scale low- and zero-emission fuel projects around the world. But shipping needs far greater volumes available at competitive prices and at major bunker locations.

Several small-scale biofuel and e-fuel projects are being developed around the world.

Swiss startup Synhelion expects to start commercial operations at its 1,000 mt/year synthetic fuel plant in Germany in 2028. German-Brazilian startup Atlanteo is developing a modular e-methanol production concept, with its first 20 MW plant expected to produce around 10,000 mt/year.

European Energy’s Kassø e-methanol facility in Aabenraa, Denmark, which is already operating, produced 4,974 mt of e-methanol in the first half of 2026, against a planned capacity of 32,000 mt/year. The company is also planning a 48,000 mt/year e-methanol plant in Québec, Canada, with Greenfield Global.

ENGIE is planning a biomethane production facility at the HAROPA port complex in France, with an expected output of 7,000 mt/year intended for CMA CGM’s LNG-capable fleet.

Smaller-capacity projects can help developers test technologies, identify production challenges and establish commercial supply chains. But proving a concept works is one thing. Making it work at scale to meet potential demand is another.

A large ocean-going vessel can consume thousands of mt/year of fuel. That puts the output of a 1,000 mt/year plant into perspective. Even a 10,000 mt/year facility could typically serve only a limited number of vessels, depending on their size and fuel consumption.

And shipping is hardly the only customer waiting at the door. A number of low- and zero-emission fuel producers are diversifying the allocations across multiple sectors, including aviation, road transport, chemicals and fertilisers, leaving several industries competing for the same molecules.

Then comes the cost of getting that fuel to ships.

Producing renewable fuel at a competitive price doesn’t automatically make it a viable marine fuel option. Transport, storage and physical delivery costs can push up the final bunker price, particularly when production facilities are located far from major bunkering ports.

Longer transport distances could also increase associated emissions, potentially reducing the environmental benefits of switching to cleaner fuels.

This is where the distinction between scaling production and scaling supply becomes important.

Some developers intend to expand existing facilities, while others are pursuing networks of smaller plants.

Atlanteo, for instance, plans to replicate its modular facilities in locations with suitable renewable energy and agricultural resources. Synhelion has outlined plans for larger plants in Germany and Morocco.

Both approaches could increase production capacity. But the real commercial test is whether that fuel can reach ocean-going vessels in sufficient quantities without logistics costs undermining its appeal.

None of this diminishes the importance of smaller projects. They provide an opportunity to test technologies and work through practical challenges before committing to larger investments.

But a successful pilot is only the beginning.

For renewable fuels to make a meaningful contribution to deep-sea shipping, producers must eventually develop supply chains capable of delivering sufficient volumes at workable prices to the ports where vessels actually bunker.

In other alt fuels news this week, Frontier Fuels has chartered a barge for B100 deliveries on the Elbe, for supplying ships at five ports, including Hamburg and Cuxhaven. The barge, Lina, will carry only B100 (100% biofuel), the company said. It will also deliver to ships in Stade, Kiel and Brunsbüttel.

The VO Chidambaranar (VOC) Port Authority will commence methanol bunkering at the port by the end of November. The port’s methanol bunker infrastructure comprises an onshore storage facility connected to a jetty through a 2.8-km pipeline for shore-to-ship fuel transfers.

US LNG bunker supplier REV LNG completed an LNG bunkering operation for Siem Car Carriers’ vessel Aristotle, marking the first such operation at the Port of Davisville in Rhode Island. The truck-to-ship operation also marks the first LNG fuelling of a car carrier in the US Northeast, according to REV LNG.

title: IBIA 2026: Don't Expect Agreement on IMO NZF to Spell End of EU ETS — Ship & Bunker

This forced compliance exposes the industry's reactive strategy, where genuine deep decarbonization too often remains a distant, unfulfilled promise.

title: Shipping sector backs an International Maritime Organization (IMO) climate deal, but not all of the details
summary: Major shipping companies and their associations publicly endorse an IMO climate deal, but their "support" hinges on weakening critical components. Industry players are actively pushing for softer carbon pricing, diluted fuel standards, and favorable emissions accounting, avoiding specific commitments post-postponement. This predictable maneuver risks another toothless IMO agreement, ensuring continued excessive HFO usage and further delaying genuine decarbonization efforts.
content:
New analysis from the global think tank InfluenceMap confirms, with detailed evidence, broad public support across the shipping and fuels sectors for a climate deal at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). However, differing advocacy positions on key components of the framework, including the carbon price, fuel standard, and rules for counting fuel emissions, threaten to weaken the proposed framework as negotiations resume this month, ahead of MEPC 85 (from 30 November) and the resumed adoption session on 4 December.

InfluenceMap identified high-level support for the IMO Net Zero Framework (NZF) from 13 companies and industry associations. Companies and industry associations alike have emphasized the need for a global framework to provide regulatory certainty for the industry’s energy transition, and reaffirmed their support for the IMO as global regulator. The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), which represents over 80% of the world’s merchant fleet, and the World Shipping Council (WSC), which represents 90% of global liner shipping capacity, in 2025 urged governments to adopt the NZF as a “carefully balanced regulatory package”. European Shipowners (ECSA) has called global regulation essential “to deliver the energy transition of international shipping.” Other companies and associations that have shown support include CMA CGM, COSCO Shipping, Hapag-Lloyd, Moller-Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Company, FuelsEurope, Ipieca, Renewable Fuels Association, Shell, and SEA-LNG.

However, in the past year, industry’s support for the Net-Zero Framework has become more cautious. Since adoption was postponed in October 2025, the main shipping associations, including the ICS and WSC, have avoided naming the framework, instead asking governments to “consider all options.” They have not proposed specific changes, but this softer messaging leaves room for a weaker deal. A significant risk remains that the IMO will deliver an agreement that undermines the global shipping industry’s ability to decarbonize, with less ambitious proposals creating a landing zone that moves the IMO away from the net-zero trajectory it agreed to in its 2023 GHG Strategy: net-zero emissions by or around 2050, with cuts of at least 20% by 2030 and 70% by 2040.

The NZF has two linked parts, a fuel standard that tightens over time and a carbon price on ships that miss it, both resting on life-cycle rules for counting each fuel’s emissions. InfluenceMap found engagement on these key elements from 4 industry associations: ICS, WSC, Ipieca and SEA-LNG. WSC supported all three elements. ICS broadly supported a carbon price but pushed for a weaker fuel standard ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025. Since then, Ipieca and SEA-LNG, representing oil and gas and LNG fuel interests, have advocated against strict GHG life-cycle rules.

Carbon Pricing: ICS and WSC both backed a carbon price, but ICS argued for a low and narrow one. Ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025, ICS proposed a carbon price of USD 10–20 per tonne of CO2e, charged only on emissions from burning fuel, not from producing it. WSC backed a carbon price set high enough to make clean fuels competitive, illustrated at USD 74 per tonne in 2030. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025.

Fuel Standard: WSC backed an ambitious standard; ICS argued for a weaker one. In 2024-25, ICS backed a fuel standard but proposed a 30% cut in fuel GHG intensity by 2040, less than half the 65% in the approved NZF. WSC supported the IMO’s fuel standard and its GHG intensity targets. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025. SEA-LNG opposed proposals that fuels should meet a minimum GHG threshold to count towards the standard.

Accounting Rules: Ipieca and SEA-LNG pushed to lower fossil fuels’ counted emissions; WSC backed stricter accounting. Since April 2025, Ipieca has advocated for replacing the IMO’s cautious default values for fossil fuels with averages and letting certificates stand in for clean power. SEA-LNG argued that LNG’s production emissions are lower than regulators assume. Both would make it easier for LNG-powered ships to comply.

The sharpest divide is between sectors. Shipping associations have broadly backed the framework’s core elements. Meanwhile, oil and gas sector groups have publicly supported the NZF while pushing at the IMO for accounting rules that would make fossil fuels, particularly LNG, count as cleaner. These rules decide how strict the framework is in practice, so loosening them could weaken it without changing the headline targets. The accounting rules are on the agenda when the IMO’s working group meets on 23–27 November.

Notably, InfluenceMap’s research found that support for the NZF often comes at the expense of regional regulations currently in force. ICS, WSC, SEA-LNG, and European Shipowners (ECSA) have leveraged support for a global framework to advocate against the FuelEU Maritime regulation and the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), calling for the review, harmonization, or withdrawal of these EU-level regulations following the passage of the IMO NZF, despite these rules already being in force and central to meeting EU climate targets.

title: Charting the Course: How to Navigate Maritime Shipping
summary: While the shipping industry focuses on navigating geopolitical disruptions and port congestion, there's a glaring omission of any strategy to mitigate the environmental impact of these challenges. Extended voyages due to Red Sea instability and Strait of Hormuz threats directly translate to higher fuel consumption, exacerbating carbon emissions from the fleet, particularly from HFO-burning ships. Industry solutions like 'carrier alliances' and 'digitization' are mere operational bandages, offering no credible plan to address the inevitable surge in carbon intensity and FuelEU Maritime compliance risks from these longer routes.
content:
Between shifting trade policies, geopolitical hot spots, port congestion, and rising regulations, ocean shipping is anything but smooth sailing. By leveraging carrier alliances and technology innovations, and implementing smart booking strategies, shippers can stay on course.

Maritime shipping, while never easy, has become even more difficult. “Ocean carriers and shippers are navigating geopolitical disruption, shifting trade policies, port congestion, weather-related impacts, and the need for more predictable service across global trade lanes,” says Claudia Kattan, vice president, logistics, for Central America, Mexico and Panama with Crowley, a maritime, energy, and logistics solutions company.

However, ocean carriers are working in multiple ways to boost their own resilience and reliability, including by forming alliances and investing in digitization. Shippers also can take steps to work more productively with carriers by developing a broad network of partner relationships and extending booking times, among other actions.

Geopolitical Tension Creates Challenges

Each year, ships move about 280 million containers across the world’s oceans, transporting roughly 80% of international trade when measured by volume, according to the World Shipping Council.

The most immediate disrupter to these journeys is geopolitical route instability, says Michael Augustin, principal director and ocean freight lead with Accenture. This instability impacts lead times, inventory buffers, supplier allocation, and network design. Both carriers and shippers now plan around the increasingly frequent geopolitical disruptions, rather than wait them out.

In the Red Sea, the Houthis have seized several islands, boosting their ability to control this important shipping route. Transit through the Suez Canal, which connects the Mediterranean and Red Seas, remains about 70% below 2023 levels.

The threat of confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz has prompted a 95% drop in traffic. Many ships now are diverting around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

The Panama Canal has become another pressure point, says Ian Wilson, principal analyst with Everstream Analytics. In late summer 2026, the Panama Canal Authority announced restrictions to the number of vessels that can move through the canal, citing a lack of rainfall and lower watershed inflows, as well as the forecast of a severe El Niño event.

Together, these challenges have depressed global shipping schedule reliability to around 56%, says Melissa Curry, vice president of global at NFI. They also lead to congested ports and localized shortages of specialized equipment, such as refrigerated trailers.

Because of the disruptions, carriers often need to balance excess capacity in some parts of their networks, with strained capacity elsewhere, says Priya Anand, director of global logistics services with Jabil, a provider of engineering, supply chain, and manufacturing solutions. At times, carriers have canceled scheduled voyages, which can artificially boost demand.

Spot rates are also up, often dramatically. The Shanghai-Los Angeles spot rate jumped 185% between September 2025 and September 2026, according to Wayfindr, a logistics provider. Similarly, the spot rate for the Shanghai-New York route was up 161% over the same period, Wayfindr says.

Carrier disruptions are particularly difficult because they rarely affect only the ocean legs of shipper supply chains, says Michael Britton, head of North America market, ocean products, with Maersk.

When vessels are rerouted or schedules change, the effects often ripple through transportation, warehousing, inventory planning, and other operations. For instance, shippers may boost inventory levels to ensure they have enough to cover the extended lead times.

Tariffs Have an Impact

At the same time, ongoing shifts in tariff policy make costs and demand patterns hard to predict, Augustin says. Shippers often accelerate purchases ahead of anticipated tariff deadlines, creating artificial spikes in volume that are then followed by aggressive pullbacks. These swings impact carriers’ revenue and complicate their network planning. They also upend shippers’ ability to plan.

As manufacturers have diversified at least some operations from China to other parts of the world, they’ve also generated new logistics requirements around ports, customs capabilities, lead times and other functions.

“Sourcing footprints are changing faster than transportation networks and infrastructure can adapt,” Augustin says. This often sparks capacity mismatches.

Another challenge is the “compounding event phenomenon,” Wilson says. When multiple disruptions hit at about the same time, the impact of each is magnified. For instance, Typhoon Saudel hit areas of China a few weeks after Typhoon Dolphin. Some port operators hadn’t cleared congestion from Dolphin before Saudel hit, making the jobs even more difficult.

Expanding regulations are also driving up shipping costs. For example, beginning in January 2026, the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) required ocean carriers to cover 100% of applicable emissions to, from, and within the EU. This effectively adds $50 to $100 per metric ton to fuel costs on European routes.

FuelEU Maritime further penalizes vessels using conventional fuels. While carriers are investing in LNG, methanol, and ammonia-ready vessels, their investments also drive up costs. “This is a structural freight cost floor that shippers need to budget for, independent of whatever rate volatility the market delivers,” Augustin says.

Best Thing Since Water

While the challenges are daunting, carriers are taking multiple steps to address them. A key one is the formation of global alliances between carriers (see box for more information). Through the alliances, the carriers remain competitors but share vessel space.

Maersk has indicated that one such alliance, The East-West Network, is “the best thing to happen to shipping since water.” This network is made possible by Gemini Cooperation, the name given to the collaboration between Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd. Gemini achieved schedule reliability above 90%, according to Hapag-Lloyd.

When individual routes are disrupted, carriers that operate within a coordinated alliance often have more flexibility to redeploy capacity, consolidate sailings, and protect schedule integrity than do carriers operating independently.

The alliances aren’t a panacea. Taking a hub-and-spoke approach, as many alliances do, can boost schedule reliability, but it can mean the cargo will take a more circuitous journey and require transshipping, says Guillaume Bournisien, managing director, freight forwarding, USA and Canada, with GEODIS.

The concentration of carriers can also lead to fewer independent options on major trade lanes, reducing shippers’ leverage in negotiations.

In addition, data standardization between ocean carriers is currently a question mark, Anand says. As a result, data may work differently, even between carriers within the same network. Shippers then need to create models to standardize the data so it is useful in decision-making.

The Digital Container Shipping Association (DCSA) does offer a reference page that shows which carriers have adopted which standards, says Lauren Beagen, chief executive officer and founder of The Maritime Professor.

In addition to forming alliances, some carriers are boosting regional connectivity. Crowley, for instance, recently added a weekly express service connecting Port Houston with markets in Guatemala and Honduras. This will help customers move goods efficiently across the Central America, U.S. and Caribbean trade lanes, with fewer handoffs, plus a broader equipment mix.

Digitization Takes Hold

As the “arteries of logistics” become increasingly fragile, and as more events disrupt planning, shippers need transparency. “Maritime is definitely the next industry that is up for an IT revolution,” says Karsten Schmidt, director of smart containers with Hapag-Lloyd. Information technology can provide this transparency.

Hapag-Lloyd is equipping its fleet of two million dry containers with Internet of Things (IoT) devices that frequently transmit location and condition updates. Shippers can leverage data from the devices, such as a container’s estimated arrival time at a warehouse, to enhance production and labor planning, Schmidt says.

Hapag-Lloyd also is working with ERP providers to ensure that data from the devices can be integrated within their systems.

The devices can be leveraged in other ways, as well. One company that works with raw materials plans to use the devices to reduce financing costs, Schmidt says, noting that a significant challenge in cargo financing is proving the cargo actually exists. An IoT tracker on a container can show this, as well as the cargo’s location. Having this information available may help companies reduce financing costs.

Another application of digitization, electronic bills of lading, could help mitigate cargo theft, as they’re generally less able to be modified than their paper counterparts, Beagen says. Across the industry, the adoption of electronic bills of lading could save $6.5 billion in direct costs, and enable up to $40 billion in global trade, according to a 2022 McKinsey study. However, not all countries currently have legal frameworks that formally acknowledge electronic bills of lading, the International Trade Centre notes.

While ocean carriers remain focused on the sea, many are adding services that can help shippers once their cargo reaches land.

Crowley, for instance, offers inland transportation, warehousing, and logistics services, Kattan says. Shippers can use the ocean service alone or add logistics support as market conditions, cargo requirements, and delivery timelines change.

Multiple carriers have been acquiring freight forwarding, customs brokerage, warehousing, and last-mile capabilities. If something does go wrong, shippers “have one throat to choke,” Augustin says.

On the other hand, the more bundled a relationship, the harder it is to switch out individual services or benchmark them against competitors’ offerings. Also, shippers’ negotiating leverage can erode over time.

Along with the actions that carriers are taking, shippers can do their part to work productively with their ocean transportation partners. A starting point is understanding how spiking fuel costs, additional surcharges, and other market shifts impact their own costs per unit, says Nick Bartlett, co-founder and director with Wayfindr.

Questions to ask include:

Should I ship?

Should I wait?

Should I front load?

Should I look at alternative fulfillment models?

Too Little, Too Late

Addressing these questions often requires some visibility into the carrier’s network. Without it, shippers often learn about variances, such as carriers canceling scheduled sailings or skipping planned port calls, perhaps to recover their schedules, too late to proactively adjust inventory, transportation, or customer commitments, Bournisien says.

The goal is to evaluate total costs of each carrier. A cheaper booking on a less-reliable carrier can end up costing more if it becomes necessary to add inventory because the schedule can’t be trusted.

“Shift the procurement lenses from price to reliability,” Bournisien says.

Building relationships with multiple ocean carriers and understanding the options they offer also helps when a shipper plans to enter new markets or consider new services. They’re not starting from zero, Beagen says.

Also, the deeper the carrier network that a shipper is using, the wider the benchmark for evaluating spot pricing. And while some shippers assume they lack leverage when negotiating with carriers, “everyone’s got leverage at some point,” Bartlett says, adding that shippers just need to know when to try to use it. For instance, if a vessel is rerouted with no notice, the carrier should face a penalty or other consequence.

Multiple Choice

Along with building a broad carrier network, shippers benefit by developing multiple options for different transportation modes, Anand says. If, for instance, ocean transport won’t move products as quickly as needed, a shipper might replace a segment of the trip with rail.

Given the current environment, Curry recommends shippers extend booking lead times to three to four weeks and build buffers of 10 to 14 days into their cargo-ready dates. And while shippers should maintain baseline cargo contracts for core stability, they’ll want to keep some portion of their volume flexible so they’re positioned to capitalize on potential post-peak rate adjustments and spot market capacity in late 2026.

Because the forces reshaping ocean freight, including geopolitical tension and shifting trade policies, are becoming structural in nature, ocean freight should no longer be managed in isolation. “It has become an integral component of sourcing, inventory and network strategy,” Augustin says.

Carrier-shipper relationships need to evolve into ones that are strategic, data-driven, and built around shared resilience.

Controlling Global Trade Routes

While individual cargo ships dominate the horizon, the real power on the water lies in shared networks. To maximize capacity and keep global trade moving, the world’s top ocean carriers pool their vessels into mega-alliances—or, in one notable case, leverage sheer size to chart a solo course (see sidebar). Here are the major players driving global shipping today.

OCEAN ALLIANCE

Primary Carriers: CMA CGM, COSCO, OOCL, Evergreen

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: Roughly 29%

Description: Massive capacity and broad networks; can run dense east-west networks

GEMINI COOPERATION

Primary Carriers: Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: 21%

Description: Focus is on schedule reliability and operational stability through controlled connections

PREMIER ALLIANCE

Primary Carriers: ONE, HMM, Yang Ming

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: 18%

Description: Competitive on trans-Pacific and intra-Asian routes; network breadth and frequency through pooled capacity

INDEPENDENT

Carrier: MSC

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: 18%

Description: As an independent, can be less complex than an alliance

MSC Goes It Alone

While mega-alliances dominate much of container shipping, Mediterranean Shipping Co. (MSC) has charted a radically different course. Since August 2020, the Swiss carrier has acquired 500 secondhand ships, doubling its fleet capacity from 3.8 million to nearly 7.4 million TEU and capturing more than 21% of global liner capacity.

Combined with an aggressive newbuilding program, this rapid expansion propelled MSC past Maersk to become the world’s largest containerline. Crucially, that sheer fleet size has enabled a feat no major competitor has attempted: operating principal east-west trade lanes independently, without belonging to a global vessel-sharing alliance.

Following the conclusion of its 2M partnership with Maersk, MSC launched a standalone global network, demonstrating that unmatched scale can replace traditional partnership models.

title: IMO may codify alternative net-zero bunker rules in 2027: US FMC
summary: The IMO's "net-zero" bunker framework continues to drift, with final codification now optimistically slated for 2027, thanks to strong US opposition. The US Federal Maritime Commission rejects mandatory carbon bills, citing potential annual costs of $53 billion-$265 billion for the industry. This extended delay prioritizes financial concerns over immediate, tangible measures to reduce shipping's carbon intensity.
content:
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) may start forming consensus around an alternative Net-Zero Framework (NZF) in the coming weeks before hammering out its final text in 2027, US Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella said Nov. 11.

The UN agency is due to hold meetings Nov. 23-Dec. 4 to discuss the framework, after member states last year voted to delay its adoption by a year amid fierce US opposition.

“I hope we’re going to come to some sort of landing spot,” DiBella told Platts on the sidelines of the International Bunker Industry Association’s annual convention in New York City.

“I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027, it will be codified. But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus,” DiBella said.

The comments from the top US maritime regulator came after Japan, Panama, and some other countries proposed several alternatives to the NZF, which, in its current form, would place a mandatory cost on maritime greenhouse gas emissions from 2028 to promote a low-carbon bunker transition.

The US has estimated that the framework would cost the shipping industry $53 billion-$265 billion annually while arguing the incremental expenses would be ultimately passed on to businesses and consumers.

“We have the potential to take remedial action against the flag states that support it, that deliver cargo to the US,” DiBella said, referring to the FMC’s remit. “As the largest consumer of imported goods, we will face the biggest penalties. We don’t need additional inflationary measures on our cargo.”

But Washington would be open to what it believes to be a commercially realistic, technology-neutral NZF with achievable emissions targets, voluntary market-based compliance, and no mandatory carbon bills collected by the IMO, the US has suggested.

“The United States is working toward a consensus on something so that industry can make the necessary investments [in alternative fuels] and move ahead,” DiBella said.

Gas pathway

DiBella has displayed a favorable attitude toward LNG and bio-LNG and previously said in a web post that based on her personal view, the fuels could meet over 60% of global maritime bunker demand by 2050, and that the US is well positioned to supply the fuels as the world’s top LNG exporter, which could draw investments in increasing bio-LNG output with a “well-designed global fuel standard.

“The infrastructure is there to support it globally … I lean very heavy on the infrastructure side and what’s available and what’s realistic,” she told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy.
