title: Korean partnership’s carbon capture proposal selected as basis for IMO’s future safety guidelines
summary: The IMO has selected a Korean proposal as the foundation for future safety guidelines concerning onboard carbon capture systems (OCCS). This regulatory step, however, risks becoming a greenwashing distraction, offering distant technological promises instead of immediate, verifiable emission reductions. Real progress demands actual carbon intensity cuts today, not just frameworks for systems that may enable continued high-carbon fuel usage for vessels failing their CII ratings.
content:
A leading Korean public-private partnership comprising 10 maritime organizations has reached a major milestone in the development of international safety guidelines for onboard carbon capture and storage system (OCCS) after the proposal jointly developed by its members was selected as the base document for further development at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

At the IMO’s 12th session of the Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (CCC 12), the working group agreed to use the proposal from the Korean partnership as the basis for developing interim OCCS safety guidelines, incorporating elements of a separate proposal from the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS).

Established in April 2026, the partnership is led by Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, with Korean Register (KR) overseeing regulatory development. Its members include HMM, Samsung Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, Hyundai Heavy Industries Power Systems, HI Air Korea, PANASIA and the Korea Research Institute of Ships & Ocean Engineering (KRISO).

Drawing on the partners’ operational, shipbuilding, manufacturing and research expertise, KR consolidated their technical contributions into a single regulatory proposal, which was submitted to the IMO through the Ministry.

CCC 12 also agreed to establish the Correspondence Group on GHG Safety under Korea’s coordination to advance the guidelines. Joonghun Kim from KR’s Convention & Legislation Service Team has been named coordinator of the group and will bring together contributions from IMO Member States and international organizations to develop common safety requirements, with technology-specific annexes to be considered if time permits. The group will report its progress to CCC 13 in 2027.

Kyung-bok Kim, Executive Vice President of KR, said: “The practical experience, knowledge and expertise of the entire 10-member partnership have led to an important milestone in the development of OCCS safety standards at an IMO level. Our next step is to bring contributions from Member States and international organizations together to develop workable safety requirements.

“By leading the development of OCCS standards, Korea is leading the charge in the global decarbonization of the maritime industry, helping to ensure that safe, workable OCCS solutions become a practical reality for vessels worldwide,” he added.

The proposal builds on Korea’s multi-year OCCS development work, including raising safety concerns about the location of onboard CO₂ storage tanks in 2023 and proposing initial safety guidelines in 2024.

It also draws on technical assessments and operational experience associated with HMM Mongla, which was fitted with an OCCS solution in 2024 as part of a joint project involving HMM, Samsung Heavy Industries, PANASIA and KR. Ongoing risk assessments based on the vessel’s OCCS design identified 64 hazard scenarios, helping to inform the development of practical shipboard safety requirements.

The proposed guidelines address how OCCS equipment can be safely integrated with a vessel’s structure, layout and machinery systems. They cover practical safety considerations including CO₂ handling and storage, leakage prevention, emergency response and the safe transfer of captured carbon ashore. These requirements are intended to address not only the capture equipment itself, but also its interaction with other onboard systems and day-to-day vessel operations.

The framework retains a technology-neutral main body covering common safety requirements, alongside separate annexes addressing hazards specific to different OCCS technologies. This approach allows different capture methods, including chemical absorption, membrane separation and mineralization, to be considered without favoring a particular technology, while enabling requirements to evolve as further evidence becomes available.

Speaking about the importance of reflecting real-world operational experience in the proposed guidelines, members of the Korean partnership highlighted the need for practical standards that reflect the realities of running OCCS systems at sea.

Youngsun Kim, Senior Vice President, Director of Technology & Innovation Institute, HMM Co., Ltd., said: “Shipowners need standards covering safe operation, maintenance and offloading, not capture performance alone. It was important to be able to reflect actual operating conditions from an early stage of international guideline development.”

Ho-ki Lee, Vice President at Samsung Heavy Industries, said: “At CCC 12, we saw growing consensus around onboard carbon capture as a practical option for decarbonizing shipping. Drawing on our experience in shipbuilding and OCCS demonstration, we will contribute to international safety guidelines that enable carbon capture systems to operate safely and efficiently on board ships.”

Yoon-Sik Hwang, Vice President at Hanwha Ocean, said: “This joint proposal is particularly meaningful because it brings together expertise from shipbuilding, shipping, marine equipment and classification. Hanwha Ocean will continue contributing to the development of international safety guidelines, drawing on its demonstration experience and technical capabilities to accelerate the commercialization of onboard carbon capture technology.”

Sangmin Park, Senior Vice President at HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, said: “The acceptance of the Korean-led proposal on interim OCCS safety guidelines is a meaningful achievement towards the commercialization of onboard carbon capture technology. Drawing on the experience accumulated through OCCS technology development, HDKSOE will contribute to international safety guidelines to support the safe application of OCCS on ships.”

Jeongsu Seo, Executive Director at HI AIR KOREA, said: “Safety functions must be capable of being tested and verified in the field. Drawing on our experience in developing and demonstrating mineralization-based capture technology, we will contribute to practical safety standards for both newbuildings and retrofits by linking that experience to leak detection and emergency shutdown requirements.”

title: The Demand-Side Case: Scope 3 Pressure and Maritime Decarbonisation Gap
summary: The IMO's MEPC 83 again failed to implement a global $150-per-tonne CO₂ shipping levy, demonstrating its continued inability to enforce meaningful decarbonisation. However, corporate Scope 3 emissions targets are now forcing logistics providers to demand genuine carbon intensity data from their shipping partners. This external pressure, not bureaucratic talks, will expose which ships are still burning excessive HFO and exceeding their CII ratings.
content:
In April 2025, the International Maritime Organization's (IMO) 83rd Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting ended without consensus on a global shipping levy. The proposed Net Zero Fund (NZF), a $150-per-tonne charge on shipping CO₂ emissions projected to raise some $120 billion a year to fund further decarbonisation projects, remains unagreed for now.

The noise declared progress on maritime decarbonisation had stalled, but there is an underlying signal that tells a different story, with quiet progress in procurement departments from Stockholm to São Paulo to Seoul.

Corporate sustainability teams asked the same question of their logistics providers: what is the carbon intensity of the ship carrying my goods, and what are you doing to reduce it?

Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) commitments to reduce Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions were already operative. They just didn't need a UN agreement.

But what is that signal, and how strong is it? Here we quantify that signal and what it means for shipping markets, and why it matters now, even at a fraction of the NZF's scale

Scope 3: the new charter conversation

Scope 3 refers to indirect emissions from across a company's value chain, up and downstream of its own operations. They are the least visible and least actioned part of corporate climate commitments.

Scope 3 are also, on average, 26 times larger than a company's direct (Scope 1 and 2) emissions. For a fashion retailer, a pharmaceutical company, or an electronics manufacturer, the largest single component of Scope 3 is usually transportation, and that transportation usually includes shipping.

The GHG Protocol's Category 4 (upstream transportation and distribution) and Category 9 (downstream transportation) capture this exposure. Until recently, few companies reported on them with any rigour, fewer still tying targets to them.

That has changed. In September 2025, 8.8% of all companies (1,046 of the full SBTi database of 15,564 companies) included SBTi-validated near-term targets naming upstream transportation with the top sectors, food and beverage (152 companies), textiles and apparel (91), pharmaceuticals (89), and retail (70). These are, without exception, the largest volume shippers of containerised cargo on the planet.

And these are not soft commitments. SBTi validation requires targets to be consistent with 1.5°C or well-below 2°C pathways, independently reviewed, and publicly disclosed. If a major food group or a global apparel brand has an SBTi-validated Cat 4 target, it is legally and reputationally exposed if it cannot demonstrate progress. That exposure flows directly to the choice of carrier.

The fleet cannot yet deliver

So the demand for lower emission shipping is there, but there’s a problem. The fleet cannot absorb it.

The IMO's revised GHG Strategy requires international shipping to cut its carbon intensity by 40% from 2008 levels by 2030, dropping from a fleet average of approximately 100 grams of CO₂ per tonne-mile to around 72 by 2030. That 28% gap must be closed in less than four years, across 165,000 active vessels.

In the first year of Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) reporting in 2023, 30% of the active fleet attained the two lowest grades, D or E, which trigger improvement plans and, eventually, commercial consequences. That is roughly 49,500 ships.

The supply response is modest. Of those 165,000 active vessels, just 1.5% (2,493 vessels) could run on alternative fuels. Of the global orderbook of 10,355 vessels, by early 2024, only 14% of ordered new tonnage was alternative-fuel-ready (UNCTAD RMT 2024). At the current pace, replacing the D/E-rated fleet would take nearly five years, and most use conventional fuel.

A year ago that premium barely existed. Today it is a negotiating variable on every long-term charter. And clients with Scope 3 targets are ever more willing to pay it, or require it as a condition of contract.

Quantifying the pressure

We modelled three scenarios for how 1,046 Cat 4-committed companies translate into shipping market demand. The scenarios bracket the plausible range of shipper behaviour given different levels of procurement engagement.

Passive: the conservative floor

Five per cent of committed companies actively specify vessel performance in charter decisions. The rest report but do not act. At a shadow carbon price of $20 per tonne CO₂ equivalent, the implied annual demand signal on containerised trade is worth approximately $0.7 billion. This is the floor and already happening.

Active Procurement: the base case

Twenty-five per cent of committed companies specify eco-vessels, consistent with observed behaviour among Sea Cargo Charter signatories. After a 40% efficiency discount, accounting for vessel availability constraints and contract timing gaps, the implied signal on 2.335 billion tonnes of containerised trade, at a shadow price of $45 per tonne, is approximately $4.7 billion per year.

MBM / Book & Claim: the upside

An additional 10% engage via Book & Claim certificates or nascent maritime emissions trading mechanisms, adding to the Active scenario. After a 60% efficiency discount (the Book & Claim market for shipping is still thin), the combined signal reaches approximately $10.7 billion per year.

These are shadow carbon costs: the value shippers assign to emissions when choosing between vessels. No money changes hands, and there is no tax or surcharge but these numbers influence real chartering decisions. A shipper using a $45 carbon price and accepting a 10-12% eco-premium is making the same basic calculation as under a carbon levy, just on a voluntary basis.

What the NZF stalemate means

The IMO NZF is a supply-side mechanism that would change the economics for every ship at $150 per tonne of CO₂, raising $120 billion a year to find alternative fuel infrastructure in developing countries and de-risked newbuild orders at a scale that the market cannot achieve alone.

Scope 3 pressure is demand-side, working through very different levers, the shipper's procurement decision, the charter contract, the sustainability questionnaire, the annual CDP disclosure.

However, the Scope 3 signal covers only a fraction of seaborne trade, primarily containerised cargo where shipper brand exposure is highest. It seldom reaches bulk carriers where cargo owners rarely have a Scope 3 alignment incentive. Scope 3 incentives are uneven, voluntary, and unenforceable. When it eventually comes, NZF, will do things Scope 3 pressure structurally cannot.

But the SBTi commitment pipeline is growing at approximately 35% per year. The first wave of Cat 4 targets, set in 2021 and 2022, hit reporting deadlines in 2025 and 2026. Companies setting 30% reduction targets with a 2025 base year will be audited against those targets imminently. That creates a step-change in the urgency of Scope 3 procurement, independent of anything IMO does.

What Scope 3 means for shipowners and financiers

For shipowners, eco-efficient vessels now carry a demonstrable commercial premium, and that premium has a structural driver, the Scope 3 commitment pipeline, that will intensify over the next three years regardless of IMO outcomes. Vessels with verified emissions intensity data, GLEC-compliant reporting, and CII ratings of A or B will be the only choice for the committed shipper segment.

The 36 Poseidon Principles signatory banks represent some 75% of global ship finance and measure their portfolios' carbon alignment annually. An owner’s access to competitive financing increasingly depends on its emissions profile. The Scope 3 and Poseidon stories are converging: the shipper's charter choice and the bank's lending decision are shaped by the same underlying decarbonisation pressure.

For financiers, the 41% of the fleet aged 25 years or more represents the most acute risk. These vessels are unlikely to retrofit economically, many facing accelerating obsolescence as the charter market polarises between compliant and non-compliant tonnage.

The combination of CII D/E ratings, Poseidon Principles portfolio pressure, and shipper Scope 3 specification requirements creates a compounding stranded-asset risk for older tonnage not yet priced into most residual value curves.

title: Shipping's $95bn fossil fuel bonfire
summary: The shipping industry burned an estimated $95 billion on fossil fuels in just nine months, a direct consequence of its unsustainable dependence and volatile markets. This colossal sum, enough to finance widespread wind propulsion, was instead wasted, offering zero return on long-term energy security or emissions reduction. This continued reliance directly exacerbates carbon intensity metrics and guarantees increasing FuelEU Maritime fines, exposing the industry's failure to genuinely decarbonize.
content:
The shipping industry has spent an estimated $95bn more on fuel since the Hormuz crisis began. That money could have financed wind propulsion across much of the world’s merchant fleet, slashing emissions and reducing exposure to future energy shocks. Gavin Allwright, secretary-general of the International Windship Association (IWSA), writes for Splash today.

The maritime shipping industry just set $95bn on fire.

Over the past nine months, geopolitical turmoil around the Strait of Hormuz has forced the sector to absorb a massive fossil fuel premium. Had that exact capital been invested into free, zero-emission wind propulsion instead of pouring it into volatile oil markets, shipowners would already be saving billions while helping to permanently secure their energy independence.

As negotiators head to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) this December, they are drawing red lines over a proposed $11bn-$12bn fund for the Net-Zero Framework. Yet, the industry just handed over nearly eight times that amount to fossil fuel suppliers since late February. This shocking amount represents a massive transfer of wealth out of the maritime sector with absolutely zero return on long-term energy security or commercial resilience.

This is my maths. Since the beginning of this recent geopolitical instability, spiking fuel costs drained an extra $340m a day from the industry throughout March alone. With the global average price of Very Low Sulphur Fuel Oil (VLSFO) surging from $500 to $810 per tonne – with other fuels spiking even higher, making the monthly fuel bill skyrocket from $12.5bn to well over $20bn. If the numbers don’t lie, this adds up to a $95bn toll simply because the industry remains dependent on fossil fuels in an increasingly unstable world and extremely volatile markets.

That lost capital could have driven vessels’ energy independence instead. Wind propulsion harnesses a globally abundant energy source delivered entirely free at the point of use. For $95bn, between 100,000 and 200,000 wind-assist retrofit systems could have been funded. That is enough to equip half the current global fleet, slash fuel consumption by 5%, and eliminate 45m tonnes of CO2e emissions every single year.

Because wind energy is free, those immediate fuel savings would unlock a further $12bn annually, providing the exact capital needed to reinvest in up to 20,000 more systems a year. By 2040, this deployment cycle would have fully paid for itself, putting that initial $95bn back into shipowners’ pockets to fund further decarbonisation.

Alternatively, that same cash could have financed 5,000 to 10,000 newbuild primary-wind vessels, fundamentally transforming the sector by cutting fuel use and emissions by up to 80% per ship.

Additionally, this evaporated capital could have fully funded a just and equitable transition for the entire maritime workforce. It could have seamlessly financed the retraining of the 600,000 seafarers who will need to operate alternative technologies and new fuels by the mid-2030s. It would have easily covered the initial $300m-$500m needed by the Pacific Blue Shipping Partnership to deliver dozens of primary wind ships to Pacific islands. With $95bn, we could have scaled this further and rolled out similar programs globally, freeing the world’s most vulnerable economies from their expensive fossil fuel dependency.

We cannot recover the billions already burned, but we can stop the bleeding. The ongoing geopolitical crises have ruthlessly exposed the devastating cost of climate inaction and fossil fuel reliance. This December, the Net-Zero Framework is up for adoption once again at IMO and would catalyse the rapid scaling of wind technology and help break the cycle.

title: Onboard carbon capture: a practical pathway for shipping?
summary: While touted as a decarbonization 'pathway,' current onboard carbon capture (oCCS) systems for ships like Eastern Pacific Shipping's *Pacific Cobalt* capture a mere 30-40% of CO₂ emissions, with larger pilots aiming for 70%. Crucially, operating these systems demands 15-30% more fuel, directly increasing the vessel's gross carbon emissions and potentially pushing its carbon intensity (CII) rating into failing territory. Such inefficiency means a '70% capture' system with a 15% fuel penalty delivers only a 44% net CO₂ reduction, making it a costly greenwashing exercise rather than a serious solution to avoid FuelEU Maritime fines, particularly for HFO-burning vessels.
content:
From first installations to commercial use

Early commercial installations show oCCS moving beyond concept and pilot-scale development, with amine-based post-combustion capture emerging as the most mature marine option. This is currently the only technology with classed commercial installations, where full-scale systems capture around 30% to 40% of CO₂ emissions. Larger pilots target about 70%.

Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Pacific Cobalt became the first classed commercial oCCS installation in 2024 under LR’s Emission Abatement Carbon Capture & Storage (EACCS) (Amine, HFO) class notation, while Solvang’s Clipper Eris is testing a full-scale system designed to capture around 70% of the CO₂ produced by its main engine. These projects add to the growing evidence that oCCS can operate at commercial scale, but its wider value depends on the emissions reductions achieved in practice.

That depends partly on the energy needed to operate the system, which can increase fuel consumption by 15% to 30% in current applications. A 70% gross capture with a 15% fuel penalty would deliver an estimated tank-to-wake CO₂ reduction of around 44%, although waste-heat recovery could reduce that penalty. The resulting emissions reduction, cost and operational impact will vary between ships, making vessel suitability central to the business case.

Finding the right ships

Panos Mitrou, LR Senior Vice President of Shipping Strategy states: “Onboard carbon capture has the potential to become an important part of shipping's decarbonisation toolkit. For the right vessel types and trades, it offers a realistic pathway to reducing CO₂ emissions and managing carbon costs while fuel supply chains, infrastructure and regulations continue to evolve.”

The strongest opportunities for oCCS are likely to be those vessels with sufficient remaining trading life and space for the equipment. The business case will also depend on how and where these vessels operate. For example, medium range and chemical tankers trading on EEA routes have frequent port calls, offering opportunities to offload captured CO₂ while EU carbon-price exposure increases the value of reducing emissions.

For LNG-fuelled vessels and LNG carriers, cold energy released during LNG vaporisation can help liquefy captured CO₂, reducing additional power requirements. Short-sea and feeder vessels could also benefit from predictable routes and regular opportunities to offload. The case for oCCS therefore depends on the technology fitting a vessel’s operating and commercial conditions.

Without these or similar conditions, the case weakens. Ships with limited trading life, little carbon-price exposure or poor access to offloading facilities will be less likely to justify the investment. Access to offloading is another critical factor because onboard storage is limited, setting a limit on how long the system can operate before captured CO₂ must be removed. Voyage length and offloading opportunities therefore directly affect how much CO₂ can ultimately be captured, making where and how a vessel operates as important as what can be installed onboard.

The decisive challenge lies ashore

For oCCS to deliver its intended benefits, captured CO₂ must enter a transport and storage network leading to permanent storage or an eligible use. Limited port reception infrastructure is a constraint, with few ports able to receive ship-captured liquefied CO₂. Many existing facilities are designed for food-grade CO₂ that may not suit exhaust-derived streams. Development is furthest ahead in north-west Europe, supported by emerging North Sea transport and storage networks, but access remains limited elsewhere.

The emissions benefit must also be recognised within relevant regulatory frameworks. The EU ETS can recognise captured CO₂ that reaches qualifying permanent storage or utilisation, while FuelEU Maritime does not yet include oCCS in its greenhouse-gas intensity calculations. The IMO is still developing a global framework covering safety, testing, verification and carbon accounting. Practically, the success of oCCS depends on infrastructure and regulation developing alongside the technology.
